#4907. The 11 Best Deodorants for Women in 2026, Tested by a Beauty Editor

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most important. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

"Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

Controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both important, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as big of an issue for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

You've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose says your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique issues. That said, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

Solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.)

Gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

Creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," says Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

In general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Important to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she says. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

That's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. For this story, I kept the above dermatologist-approved guidance in mind and carefully researched hundreds of women's deodorants and antiperspirants.

Next, I went to the Women's Health beauty closet and revisited products in my personal collection until I eventually narrowed down my list to 24 potential contenders that seemed promising. I tested these deodorants after showering and, on weekends spent indoors, I delayed showering my underarms to see how these products held up against smell and sweat. I also considered how much odor and sweat protection they provide while exercising, running errands across New York City, and wearing them on special occasions and nights out with friends.

I also considered their ease of use, how they feel on my underarms, whether they leave behind any residue (a major pet peeve of mine), and how frequently I needed to apply to remain confident in how I smell.

With that, I give you: the best women's deodorants of 2026. They are all loved by me, and some are even well-known among the dermatologists I spoke with for this story. Regardless of which deodorant you order, they all earned major snaps from me, a very hard-to-please beauty editor. The best part? They all start at just $9 and don’t leave behind embarrassing white marks on clothing. Sign me up for bulk orders!

When it comes to selecting the best overall deodorant for women, it's tough to find a winner that doesn't include aluminum. As mentioned above, aluminum is the only active ingredient approved to stop perspiration in its tracks—a major consideration. What's more, the powdery texture works double duty to absorb moisture and leave skin with a silky finish.

And like most Dove products, this stick is chock full of moisturizing ingredients so you can rest assured that this one won't dry out your skin. “I feel like this is a deodorant you can’t go wrong with," says Women's Health beauty writer Danielle Jackson. "I recently switched back to this after using some aluminum-free formulas with more subtle scents, and I’ve just found that I’m much more confident about any sort of odors being blocked when I wear it."

But the ultimate test is, Can this hold up to activity? Jackson says this Dove stick passes that test with flying colors. "I also realized that I don’t have to worry as much about it doing its job when I’m being active or working out," she says. "It lasts all day and has a powdery scent that smells great but isn’t overbearing.”

When it comes to usage, Jackson assures that the Dove antiperspirant stick glides on easily without pulling (a major downside for most other sticks) and won't leave any white marks on my skin or clothes. Talk about an A+!The one potential downside (if you can even call it that) is that some of the other products on our list have a longer-lasting dryness promise (this one will only keep you dry for 24 hours as opposed to, say, the 48 or 72 hours promised by some other brands). But if you're like me and shower frequently, that won't be an issue.Read more: Best Natural Deodorants

A Women's Health Beauty Award winner for best deodorant, this heavy-duty antiperspirant leaves me with fresher-smelling pits from the second I swipe and up to 48 hours later. Obviously, I'm not going two days without showering, but I do notice that whenever I wear this antiperspirant while enjoying HIIT exercises or on the treadmill I'm less sweaty. Now that's pretty amazing.

Secret swears their antiperspirant helps camouflage sweat caused by activity, nerves, and heat—and I think it does a solid job, especially for heat. I wore this deo regularly back when I practiced martial arts, swam, rode horses, and attempted to play tennis. I don't normally sweat heavily, but in the summer I'd definitely reach for this antiperspirant especially when commuting underground on the New York subway system. It’s still helpful during the fall and winter season when I’m bundled up in several layers.

The only thing I don't enjoy about Secret is the packaging design. It's shaped like your standard stick deodorant where I twist the bottom to help push up the creamy formula, but I noticed the turn mechanism on mine requires a little more effort than others on this list. But if you're a heavy sweater, that's a fairly minor downside—and you shouldn't let this small con deter you from this one.

I learned about this deodorant years ago through my mom, who has been using Tom's forever. I tried it during the pandemic, but stopped using it in favor of other deodorants. But, I wanted to revisit Tom's for this story—and I'm so glad that I did.

The brand recently reformulated their line of natural deodorants, and I'm obsessed with the chic new packaging and all the incredible new scents available, like Wild Lavender, North Woods, and Mountain Spring. Tom's swears the formula is still as long-lasting as ever though, with this deodorant keeping odor at bay for 48 hours. That's pretty impressive for a natural formula. Like I said earlier, I won't ever skip my daily shower (occasionally twice daily in the summer because it's that humid along the East Coast) but Tom's keeps up with my daily activities. Think long daily commutes to the office, full workdays, after work shenanigans, and so much more.

To be frank, this level of protection isn't the norm for natural deodorants, but this stick is formulated with a generous dose of glycerin and aloe to condition my skin. It's also free of artificial fragrances that can irritate sensitive noses like mine.

All this being said, this is not the formula for you if you're a heavy sweater. I'd also say the biggest bummer about this deodorant is that it doesn't glide as easily as other alternatives on this list. There's a light dragging on my underarms, but it's not a huge problem, rather a minor annoyance that shouldn't deter you from enjoying this pick.

Is anyone else flashing back to middle and high school gym class just looking at this deodorant? I know I am, but there are several reasons every girl in my PE classes all used this roll-on antiperspirant—it's so easy to use and it's virtually invisible.

Since it's an antiperspirant, Ban keeps me sweat- and odor-free and embarrassing sweat marks on my clothes are nonexistent when I roll this onto my underarms (its clear formula doesn't transfer or leave behind any marks). What I really appreciate about Ban, though, is how it's lightweight on my skin. Sometimes creamy sticks feel like they're leaving behind a clump of product onto my pits, but that's a non-issue with Ban.

One important thing to note is that this gel roll-on doesn't dry quickly. It's not a huge drawback—the waiting period is minimal—but if you're in a super rush in the morning, keep that in mind. It's also not quite as long-lasting as some of the other formulas at 24 hours, but that's not a problem for me since, again, I shower daily.

I've always preferred stick deodorants and antiperspirants because it's what I'm used to. But this Dove formula makes a compelling case for anyone who's also shopping for weightless odor and sweat protection. So how does it work? “They create a flexible film of active ingredients on your skin and remain dry,” says cosmetic chemist Perry Romanowski. Dove relies on finely milled aluminum for invisible protection, plus a special masking oil to prevent any marks from getting on my clothes.

But similar to spray sunscreens, spray deodorants and antiperspirants can get a little messy and feel hard to control, and this one is no exception. So, it's probably best to skip buying this one for someone who isn’t super clean or a preteen who might spray this a little too liberally.

As we've said before: Whole body deodorants are hugely popular right now, with all the major players getting in on this trend. It's a smart idea—just 2 percent of our sweat glands exist in our underarms, so it's clear the need for all-over odor solutions is great.

This formula, with tapioca starch and mandelic acid, works to acidify skin’s pH, preventing odor-causing bacteria from proliferating. Rub a pea-sized amount into smelly areas, including the vulva, under-boob, thigh folds, and underneath the butt cheeks. A little goes a long way here, and you can always add more as needed.

Since its launch, Lume has expanded its portfolio to include stick deodorants, wipes, body creams, body washes, and acidified cleansing bars that are pH-optimized to control odor.

You deserve a deodorant that can keep up with your active lifestyle. Who better than tennis star Sloane Stephens to create a high-performance natural whole B.O.dy deodorant. I’m a huge fan of this spray and previously named it one of the best whole body deodorants of all time.

What impresses me the most is that 24/7 Hustle is made with clean ingredients, but it doesn’t skimp on performance or irritate my skin. I wore it from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m., and was pleasantly surprised that I still smelled fresh and felt clean throughout a long travel day. It keeps up with light and intense physical activity. When I want to touch up I just swiftly spritz on this spray and I’m good to go after workout classes. No obvious residue or clammy coating that sticks to my workout sets. Woo!

So how does it work? The proprietary Deoplex Complex contains enzymes that help neutralize BO, while a botanical blend of goji berry, dragon fruit, chamomile, and ashwagandha prevents environmental damage that causes dry skin. The gentle formula also soothes my sensitive skin.

A bonus: This is the only refillable deodorant worth your hard-earned money. You can purchase a refillable pouch with enough liquid to refill your bottle nearly three times for $35. The combined price of a single refill pouch and the initial bottle is $53, while purchasing four new bottles would cost $72, resulting in a savings of nearly $20.

Dermatologist Kiran Mian, MD, previously called this one of the best natural deodorants out there because of its impressive ingredients. "It has a blend of probiotics, plant-based extracts, antioxidants, cornstarch for moisture absorption, and soothing ingredients to prevent irritation," Dr. Mian said. It’s also infused with hyaluronic acid to help hydrate my sensitive underarm skin without feeling damp throughout the day.

This is one of the best natural deodorants I’ve used in the last two years. The odor protection is comparable to traditional deodorants even during workouts and unairconditioned subway rides around New York. It definitely keeps up with sweltering summer weather along the East Coast and Euro vacations with ease.

Other reasons I’m a huge fan? It doesn’t leave behind a white cast on my clothing and it holds up nicely after exercising. Since I’m not a runner, I can’t vouch for its efficacy there, but I will say it quite literally has me covered during vinyasa yoga and mat pilates. This deodorant also holds up surprisingly well on the StairMaster and high incline walks on the treadmill.

I’m not the only fan. Tester Brigitt Earley is impressed by the texture of this deodorant, which she describes as almost like a body butter in stick form—and I agree. It doesn’t skip or tug on my skin, which has been an issue with other competitors.

Truly, the only downside with this deodorant is the price but I will say each one easily lasts me at least two months. Technically, I’m only paying $10 a month to have stink-free underarms and that’s well worth the cost to me.

If you’re familiar with any of my skincare content at Women’s Health then chances are you’ve likely seen me gush about Nécessaire products. I’m a ride-or-die fan of the brand’s body wash, exfoliator, serum, and deodorant. The line’s genius lies in the simple yet effective ingredient list. Think odor-neutralizing mandelic acid (an alpha-hydroxy acid) paired with triethyl citrate and zinc ricinoleate for odor-protection. The soft and creamy stick deodorant is also infused with soothing vitamin B3, B5, and E for hydration.Another reason I’m genuinely obsessed with this deodorant? The incredible variety of enticing scents that are noticeable enough for me to enjoy but wouldn’t overwhelm my colleagues at work.

The featured Hinoki scent is my top pick—and the one I crowned as the winner in our 2025 Skincare Awards package. Inspired by Japanese hinoki cedar trees, this earthy and woody aroma is a zen dream. It also blends notes of basil, vetiver, and magnolia, adding a spa-like serenity to my morning routine.

Another reason I love this deodorant is that it glides on seamlessly without dragging my sensitive pits. It also doesn’t leave behind white marks on my dark clothing.

TBH, it was super hard to brainstorm a true con. Nécessaire gets so many things right with this formulation. They even have a gel deodorant if that’s more your vibe. If I’m forced to name one area of improvement then it would be that there aren’t any travel-sized versions. The cylinder shape does take up a decent amount of space in my cosmetic pouch, but TBH, the formula and longevity are worth it for me. Still, if you’re a seasoned traveler who keeps things minimal, then you should consider the Anti Odorant pads instead.

Meet my favorite deodorant launch of 2026. I recently crowned it the best deodorant of the year in our annual Beauty Awards package. Here’s the TL;DR: They’re travel-friendly wipes that can be used all over the body.And now that the weather has finally warmed up, I’m heavily relying on these dermatologist-developed deodorant wipes to help me win the battle against body odor.

Their genius lies in the trifecta of odor-neutralizing enzymes, soothing aloe vera juice, and exfoliating glycolic acids that don’t sting or tingle my sensitive skin. I’ve tried the spray and love it, but the wipes are my current go-to. Since they’re individually wrapped, I can keep a few in my gym bag, work tote, and carry-on bag so my pits are quite literally covered.

TBH, I genuinely enjoy these deodorant wipes, which is why they took home a big win. However, if I must be nitpicky then it would be cool if these were available in multiple scents. However, that might easily irritate very sensitive skin types and those with sensitive noses. And honestly, the current mild scent isn’t bad—just natural and fresh, which I appreciate. Plus, it won’t accidentally clash with my perfume collection.

I've spent four years wearing this deodorant on and off and can confirm that evolvetogether hits all of the factors I look for in a deodorant. For starters, it’s made with natural ingredients. Instead of potentially harsh baking soda, aluminum, and talc, this deodorant uses tapioca starch to soak up sweat and moisture. There's also DeoPlex, a plant-based sugarcane that neutralizes bad odors, while glycerin moisturizes and prevents underarm irritation. Panthenol hydrates my underarms and helps the stick glide on easily.

Most importantly, the odor protection is on point! If you are from the South like I am then you know that even if we shad our underarms sometimes it's so hot and humid out that we inevitably get a little smelly. Not the case with evolvetogether. I've worn this deodorant walking 5Ks around my neighborhood, on the treadmill, during long cross-country flights, and I've never felt self-conscious about my smell. (My mom is also very honest and would have told me if I ever have an odor issue, so I know evolvetogether works well for me.)

As for the cons, it’s really minimal. Heavy sweaters like runners will likely need a traditional antiperspirant to keep their pits truly dry. However, for daily activities this is one of my long-time favorites.

Look, there are studies that have investigated potential links between aluminum-based antiperspirants and breast cancer or Alzheimer’s disease. "To date, no conclusive evidence supports these claims, and aluminum-based antiperspirants are generally considered safe for daily use. There is no clear evidence that they pose a significant health risk," says Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Want more proof? Well, the American Cancer Society says "there are no strong epidemiologic studies (studies in people) that link breast cancer risk and antiperspirant use, and very little scientific evidence to support this claim." Plus, this report in the National Library of Medicine details a study conducted on 130 people regarding the potential exposure to aluminum through antiperspirants, antacids, and Alzheimer's disease (AD). "For all antiperspirant/deodorant use, regardless of aluminum content, there was no association with AD,” according to the study.

#4906. Bitcoin price drops to $60K as Anthropic drops to $87 in tech sell-off

Bitcoin price strength felt pressure from falling US equities as traders reassessed AI prospects after Anthropic’s IPO.

Bitcoin dropped to $60,000 after Friday’s Wall Street open as crypto markets endured contagion from a fresh rout in tech stocks.

Data from TradingView showed Bitcoin (BTC) circling $60,000, its lowest levels in 20 weeks.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

US stocks saw continued weakness after reversing during Thursday’s trading session, with Anthropic’s debut on the Nasdaq insufficient to preserve upside momentum. ANT reached highs of $115 before reversing below the $100 mark, falling as low as $87.27 at the time of writing.

Anthropic stock five-minute chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index opened 1.2% lower, reaching 23,517 points — its lowest level since mid-April.

Nasdaq Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

In analysis on the day, crypto trading company QCP Capital drew attention to the lack of momentum in tech stocks despite Anthropic’s record IPO.

“Even Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO failed to restore confidence. Despite opening 34% above its offer price, shares faded to close up just 17%, highlighting a market increasingly unwilling to chase AI valuations,” it wrote.

QCP said that financing concerns remained throughout the AI sector in particular, with markets remaining highly sensitive to that topic throughout 2026.

“AI has become more than an equity growth story. It is increasingly a credit and liquidity story,” it continued.

Related: Bitcoin nears repeat of chart pattern that preceded 2023’s $25K retest

A flight to safety among investors saw stock markets turn lower across the board and US bond yields drop in step. The 10-year yield fell as low as 4.96% on Friday, its lowest level since Nov. 10.

US 10-year bond yield one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

A speech by Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller at the 2026 College Fed Challenge in Washington, D.C. delivered no new signals on future policy and resulted in yields reversing as traders focused on existing hawkish cues. Earlier this week, Waller told CNBC that he considered a 50-basis-point interest-rate hike in December necessary — twice the current market expectation of 25 basis points.

In his latest analysis, economist Mohamed El-Erian expressed surprise that yields had not fallen further.

“Reflecting this week’s sharp fall in stocks, where a seventh straight day of S&P 500 losses would mark its longest losing streak since 2020, the yield on the 10-year Treasury has pulled back to 4.97%,” he wrote in a blog post.

S&P 500 one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

QCP, meanwhile, saw Bitcoin price performance improving only from a combination of tech-stock stabilization, reduced volatility in rates and the return of institutional capital.

“Until then, short-covering rallies may struggle to develop into sustained upside, particularly if the Fed remains committed to tightening,” it summarized.

#4905. Hästens 2000T Mattress, Tested and Reviewed (2026)

From the moment I touched down in Sweden, the focus was on sleep. Coming off a red-eye flight from New York with only two hours of rest (three if we’re being generous), there was nothing more I wanted to do than lie down. Luckily, a Hästens mattress—the reason for my trip—awaited me at the hotel and soon provided what was perhaps the most luxurious nap I’d ever experienced.

The Swedish manufacturer, which has been making beds since 1852, sits atop the luxury market for mattresses. The brand—whose name is Swedish for “the horse’s”—has a consuming commitment to craftsmanship, and its horsehair-filled beds are handmade. That level of focus also comes with a hefty price tag, which is why the brand is perhaps best known by the general public for its presence in celebrity homes (or possibly its cameo in an Emily in Paris episode as the subject of the titular character’s latest marketing campaign). But reputation aside, Hästens knows how to make a damn good bed.

But what earns a mattress luxury status? And what is it actually like to sleep on one from Hästens? After touring the brand’s main factory in Köping, Sweden, I’ve laid my head on one of its most popular mattresses, the 2000T, for the last few months, all in the name of trying to understand how much money a good night’s sleep is worth.

To the average person, horsehair is likely not the first mattress fill material that comes to mind—if it comes to mind at all. Gel, innerspring, memory foam, cotton, or some combination of those are way more common. But horsehair has a historic precedent, having been used in beds for many periods of human history, particularly when horses were the primary mode of transportation.

Much of the present-day reason for using the material comes from a scientific point of view: Horsehair strands are naturally hollow, which Hästens claims “transports any excess heat and moisture from your body during deep sleep.” Additionally, when cut and treated, the strands form a helix shape, which works in conjunction with the metal springs in a bed for a strong base of support.

Exterior of the Hastens factory in Köping, Sweden, designed by British architect Ralph Erskine.

An hour and a half train ride northwest from Stockholm, the small town of Köping is so quiet, you might expect to see a horse roaming the streets—maybe having recently received a haircut to donate to the mattress cause. When thinking of the word factory, one may expect a loud, gigantic warehouse filled with whirring machines and assembly lines moving so quickly you can hardly see the product before it whizzes past. But the Hästens factory possessed a quite different vibe. Sure, there is still machinery and expansive production areas, but it was fairly quiet, and I felt that the energy was more akin to a pottery studio than an industrial plant: craft-forward, methodical, and with a focus on handmade artistry. In fact, my host told me that only around 100 people work in the main factory, most of whom are from the area, highlighting the company as a point of pride for the local community.

Walking into the processing room of the factory, I was greeted by a small mountain of horsehair on the floor. It looked much more like a soft version of steel wool than the shiny mane and tail I was envisioning. That’s because the hair is cut down to small strands prior to being integrated into the mattresses. The hair also goes through several disinfecting and processing treatments before it even arrives at the factory. Taking a clump between my hands, I was surprised by its springiness. (And horse girls need not fear about animal welfare: My host for the trip confirmed that their suppliers from farms around the world aren’t killing horses for their hair, the mane and tail cuttings they receive are ethically sourced.)

The blue check pattern, developed by fourth-generation company leader Jack Ryde in 1978, is synonymous with the brand. So much so that a check-laden Mercedes was waiting to drive us from the train station to the factory.

Each layer of horsehair in the mattress is fluffed by hand and placed between sheets of cotton and wool.

Every aspect of the bed creation process happens by hand: prepping the layers of wool and horsehair for the filling, arranging and securing steel springs, framing the Swedish pine base. I watched workers build each part of the bed with a devoted level of care. The only fully automated aspect of the bed manufacturing that I witnessed on my tour was stitching a pattern onto the top mattress to give it a signature tufted texture. But even that is hand-sewn on certain bed models.

Quality is tested at every step, and if something isn’t up to par, production restarts. For some models, including the Grand Vividus (at the top of Hästens range), there are only a select few craftspeople who are trained in the production process. Much of the brand’s higher price tag comes down to that heightened level of labor and care. If someone on the team is sick or is simply just working slower on a given day, the production timeline increases to accommodate the quality level that Hästens demands: perfection.

My loaned mattress also included a full set of Hästens bedding.

The 2000T is one of the brand’s best sellers, falling around the middle of their price range.

When it comes to my sleep setup, my mattress was the element that I’d been putting off upgrading for years. I only leveled up my years-old box spring with a mattress topper a few years ago. I tend to prioritize bedding when buying new duds for the bedroom, and because I’m consistently testing various sets of sheets for AD, my focus tends to be on how linens can visually transform a space rather than shift my physical experience. All to say, upgrading to a Hästens was like going from a hand-me-down sedan to a Lamborghini.

Before receiving the loaned mattress for testing, I tried out different models in person at the Manhattan flagship store in NoMad, an experience Hästens coins the Sleep Spa. As a staff member talked me through proper spinal alignment and important pressure points, I lay on various models in a Goldilocks-esque journey to see which mattress was the right fit. True to Hästens’ superlative level of service, even this part of the process felt curated. Ambient music played, lights dimmed, and I was given two pillows and a duvet for snuggling. The meditative process made me focus on how my body responded to each mattress. As a combination stomach-and-side sleeper—and someone who likes to sit on her bed—I selected the 2000T (in firm) after around an hour of sampling.

Despite being a firmer model, the 2000T still contours to my body in a way that I can only describe as cushy. The horsehair filling provides a unique springiness that the compression of memory foam or cotton can’t quite replicate. It sinks in just enough to give my shoulders enough space when I sleep on my side, but is supportive enough to keep my hips from dropping out of alignment for the nights I’m on my stomach.

As I mentioned, I often lounge on bed to read, play video games, or what have you. While facilitating sleep is the primary function of a mattress, I was keen to see how its edge control and support would stand up to this alternative usage. I was surprised by how little back pain I sustained after reading sessions that extended beyond two hours. Because of its reinforced springs at the corners and edges, I could also sit right on the edge of the mattress without feeling like I was going to roll off.

The aspect of the horsehair fill I was most intrigued to test was its claim of moisture and heat-wicking properties. I like to be fully swaddled underneath my duvet, top sheet, and sometimes even another blanket when I sleep, which can be a recipe for waking up sweaty. That hasn’t happened once with the 2000T. The foam topper on my prior bed often trapped heat, and I’d wake up in the middle of the night to rip off some of the layers of bedding in order to cool down. With the Hästens, though, I can be as greedy with my bedding as I want to be without overheating.

The ‘massage’ portion lasted about 10 minutes.

As part of their high bar of customer service, the company offers a free recalibration program from select stores to help maintain the longevity of the mattress and mitigate any compression issues. The product care program involves Hästens staffers visiting your home (typically once a year) to flip and massage the mattress—the latter consisting of a person marching back and forth across the mattress to redistribute the fill materials. I can safely say having a grown man in booties walk in circles on top of my bed for 10 minutes was one of the oddest moments of my life, but sleeping on the bed that night, I could feel the difference. While there weren’t any severe lumps formed in my two-month testing period, the process smoothed out any compression in the areas I most often lay.

Although I’ve only slept on the 2000T for around two months, I can see a noticeable change in how my body feels after a night’s rest. I struggle with hypermobility and have a family history of arthritis, so I’m on high alert about how my joints feel upon waking up in the morning. On my old bed, I typically awoke with some pain in my hips and a stiff lower back. While sleeping on the Hästens hasn’t fully eliminated any achiness, I essentially ceased needing to do the typical stretching routine I used to perform in the morning in order to get my body ready for the day.

Down pillows were provided by the brand for my loaner bed.

The structure of Hästens beds includes a top mattress and middle mattress, the former mimicking a thick topper.

As someone who has notoriously bad nighttime habits (like plentiful screen time), I had accepted I’d only be able to expect a low level of restfulness from my sleep. I was content with a solid six hours and low-level of back achiness in the morning, thinking I couldn’t consistently adjust my routine to improve my experience. Sleeping on the Hästens 2000T has changed that mindset drastically. It’s without a doubt the best mattress I’ve ever slept on.

However, it’s easy for me to say this bed is worth it because I didn’t have to pay the steep price tag of $74,780 to try it out in my home. Yes, Hästens exceeded my expectations when it came to sleep, but after the testing period ends, I don’t anticipate a sudden change in my finances that would allow me to invest in my own 2000T. Although the brand’s beds are built to last a lifetime, and we spend a third of our lives asleep, the question of how much a good night’s sleep is really worth is highly individualized.

This experience more broadly made me consider where we are most willing to invest in when it comes to our home spaces. Sure, a covetable mattress like one from Hästens may not be as flashy as other big-ticket purchases, like a giant flat screen, but I’d posit a splurge has few better use cases than on something you return to each night.

#4904. F1 Driver Isack Hadjar Has a Very Specific 9-Minute Rule

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The 22-year-old Red Bull racer on his pre-race routine, the workout he hates, and his latest obsession: GTA IV.

ISACK HADJAR HAS a problem. The 22-year-old Red Bull Formula 1 driver has finally gotten his hands on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he's slightly concerned about what that might do to his free time.

“It's going to ruin my life,” he jokes to Men's Health in the paddock ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix. He's only managed to squeeze in about 25 minutes of gameplay so far this weekend, but his verdict is already in: “It's amazing.”

For now, at least, Hadjar has his priorities straight. “I'm a professional,” he says with a smirk. “When I know it's time to go to sleep, I go to sleep.”

That level of discipline extends well beyond bedtime. In a sport that demands lightning-fast reflexes, intense concentration, and serious physical endurance, Hadjar has developed a pretty specific routine to get his brain and body ready to perform.

Take his pre-race ritual, which he has down to a science. He stretches and warms up with his trainer, including juggling and reaction-time tests to prime the brain. He listens to rap music—French, American, or British—to get himself hyped.

Then, exactly nine minutes before the race begins, he starts putting in his earpieces. “Not 10, not 11, nine," he says.

It's not a superstition or a lucky number. (That would be six, the number he drives with for Red Bull.) It’s simply what he’s found to be the perfect amount of time to get in the car and get ready to race. “I hate staying in the car doing nothing,” he says. “So for me, nine minutes is the maximum time.”

While he enjoys the pre-race preparation, there's one part of training he'd happily skip: zone 2 cardio, running at a moderate pace to power up his endurance.

“It’s just boring. I like conditioning more,” he says. To get through it, he puts on a movie, TV show, or music. “It goes by quickly in the end, but it's just, I feel like it's a waste of time. But it's very important.”

When the race is over, Hadjar's routine is considerably more relaxed. A good meal helps him switch his brain off—specifically, a burger with caramelized onions, cheddar, tomato, and lettuce. He’ll also watch anime and FaceTime his parents, especially after a good result.

And now, of course, there will be GTA VI waiting for him. Whether he'll be able to stick to that bedtime routine is another question.

Catch Hadjar in action this weekend at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, streaming live (and for free!) on Apple TV.

#4903. GTA 6 Leaker Dangles a PC Port Behind a $15 Million Crypto Pump

GTA 6 Leaker Dangles a PC Port Behind a $15 Million Crypto Pump

A notorious Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker is holding a potential PC version of the game hostage to a cryptocurrency payday, promising to release the final file needed to make a leaked build playable once its meme coin hits a $15 million market cap.

The leaker, who goes by Cyberleek, has released what it claims is a near-complete 209 GB Xbox build of GTA 6 from November 2026 via torrent, according to a report from PC Gamer.

The one piece withheld is the main executable, the file that would let modders begin emulating the game on PC, potentially bringing it to the platform long before Rockstar Games intends.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Here’s the crypto catch. Cyberleek says it will release the executable on Nov. 23 regardless, but will drop it early if its token, called CYBERLEEK, reaches a $15 million market cap. That’s half the $30 million target the leaker floated in October.

The pressure tactic doesn’t appear to be working: the token is trading around $0.002 as of the weekend, with a market cap of roughly $1.3 million, more than $13 million short of the goal. The coin is down some 20% on the week, but the numbers will fluctuate wildly given the very thin liquidity on a small cap coin.

The setup has drawn open skepticism that it’s a cash grab, or worse. Observers have warned it could be an attempt to pump the coin before a rug pull, the crypto term for abandoning a token after luring buyers in. Cyberleek has also claimed to hold a PS5 build as a fallback if the Xbox files can’t be made to work.

The episode sits at the increasingly busy intersection of crypto, piracy, and AI. Modern Xbox games are architecturally closer to PC software than PlayStation titles, and AI coding tools have accelerated the kind of decompilation work that makes fast ports plausible, the same dynamic behind a wave of AI-assisted game ports this year.

It also caps a chaotic launch window for GTA that crypto has repeatedly crashed. One trader banked around $66,000 on a GTA 6 meme coin amid ticker confusion, and the game’s disc-free, digital-only release has fueled broader debate, with GameStop’s CEO arguing that digital-only games have hurt consumers.

None of the leaked files have been independently confirmed as genuine, and there is still no official GTA 6 PC version; Rockstar, famously litigious, could respond with legal action rather than a port.

#4902. US Senate advances prediction market restrictions with DEATH BETS Act

The Senate-approved bill would ban prediction market contracts tied to war, assassination and death amid concerns over potential insider trading on military events.

The US Senate passed legislation Thursday that would prohibit federally regulated prediction markets from offering contracts tied to war, terrorism, assassination and events primarily determined by a person’s death, sending the bill to the House for consideration.

The DEATH BETS Act, introduced by Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff in March, passed by voice vote on Thursday after lawmakers adopted an amendment by unanimous consent. The bill would amend the Commodity Exchange Act to prohibit CFTC-registered exchanges from listing or clearing contracts tied to the specified events.

The legislation also covers contracts referencing US military operations and gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority to identify similar activities that would fall under the ban. Contracts would also be prohibited if, at the time of listing, they are reasonably expected to be settled primarily based on an individual’s death.

The bill was first introduced in March amid insider-trading concerns after six Polymarket traders reportedly earned $1 million betting on the timing of US strikes against Iran. Several wagers were placed just hours before the first reported explosions in Tehran, raising suspicions that traders may have had access to nonpublic information.

When introducing the bill, Schiff warned that allowing traders to profit from violent events could encourage the misuse of classified information, threaten national security and create incentives for violence.

The bill now moves to the House of Representatives, where it must pass before being sent to President Donald Trump for his signature.

#4901. The Best Shampoos for Every Hair Need and Budget, According to Experts

From L’Oréal to Oribe, these shampoos are worthy of a spot in your wash day routine.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

From sweaty runs and heat styling to product buildup, our scalps and hair need proper TLC—and that starts with a great shampoo. Our scalp is an extension of the skin on our face—it sheds dead skin cells, collects dirt and bacteria, and secretes oil and sweat, says trichologist Anabel Kingsley in our guide on how often to shampoo your hair. While the beauty community has mixed opinions on the cadence of shampooing, dermatologist DiAnne Davis, MD, recommends doing so at least once a week. The frequency varies based on your lifestyle, how quickly your hair gets greasy, your scalp health, and hair type. Since the experts advise regular shampooing, I asked the pros about how we can upgrade our healthy hair routines to preserve the expensive chemical and color treatments we enjoy at the salon.

“I always tell my clients that shampoo is mainly for your scalp, so I would start there,” says trichologist and hairstylist Courtney Foster. “You can have curly hair with an oily scalp, fine hair with a dry scalp, or color-treated hair with buildup. Hair type matters, but it doesn't tell me everything I need to know.” Choose hydrating shampoos that nourish a dry scalp, or use a lightweight shampoo with fewer moisturizing ingredients for an oily scalp.

For an oily scalp or buildup, ingredients like salicylic acid can be helpful, along with gentle cleansing agents like coco glucoside. For mineral and hard water buildup, look for chelating ingredients, as regular shampoo alone may not remove these deposits, according to Foster.

Now it’s time to think about your hair type, advises Foster. In addition to your hair texture, you’ll want to find a shampoo that’s suitable for your dry, chemically treated, damaged, or breakage-prone mane.

For dryness, humectants and conditioning ingredients such as glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and nourishing oils are your new beauty best friends. They help the hair retain moisture and feel softer and more manageable, says Foster.

For damaged hair, you’ll need shampoos packed with amino acids and bond-strengthening ingredients. “These are good for hair that has been chemically treated or excessively heat-styled,” she says of components such as hydrolyzed proteins, which can improve the feel and strength of damaged hair.

Now, if you’re dealing with frizz like I am, it likely means the hair is lacking moisture, says Foster. We’ll benefit from conditioning ingredients like polymers, silicones, oils, and humectants that help smooth the cuticle and improve manageability.

As our hair-obsessed beauty editor, I own a sizable shampoo collection. It’s 24 shampoos strong. So I started there and narrowed it down to 12 contenders. In addition to expert guidance—ingredients for a healthy scalp and cosmetic concerns like frizz—I factored in everything from their cleansing power, lather, fragrance, and feel. Did they leave my scalp parched like I just went swimming in the pool? Or did they help rebalance my scalp and prevent embarrassing flakes on my black clothing?

To help whittle down potential recommendations even further, I recruited the Women’s Health team, including beauty director Brian Underwood and deputy editor Carina Hsieh, to test these picks. Ouai Fine Hair Shampoo and Leonor Greyl immediately caught our attention and kept it. The latter even won a Women’s Health Beauty Award, and we don’t take giving out that accolade lightly.

Still, I wanted to tap into other expert picks and asked hairstylists and trichologists about the products they use at the salon and at home. Their suggestions range from a drugstore pick to a de-brassing shampoo to keep your color-treated hair looking as fresh as possible after washing.

While it sounds obvious, I factored in your budget. While my best overall pick from Oribe is on the higher end, there are several under $20 picks. And if your wallet is also looking a little tight during fun holiday adventures, I totally get it. We tested several of these shampoos, and each full-size bottle lasted us at least six weeks, with some lasting our team up to four months.

Ultimately, these are solid jumping-off points for your healthy hair routine. “One shampoo doesn’t necessarily have to do everything,” says Foster. If you use a lot of styling products, you may occasionally need a clarifying shampoo and a moisturizing shampoo for your regular wash days. “The goal is really to create a routine that keeps the scalp clean without stripping the hair.” Since you’re here, consider checking out our guides to healthy hair, including our favorite editor-tested hair masks, vitamins for hair growth, and red light therapy for hair growth. Yes, it’s a legitimate technology that’s backed by research, and dermatologists are on board.

I’d normally roll my eyes at anyone recommending a high-end shampoo as their best overall pick, but Oribe is the only shampoo I have on auto-refill. Despite its upfront cost, a single bottle of Oribe lasted me nearly four months, so it really helps stretch my cost per use.

My scalp has never been this clean with a single wash before. It helps wash away my silicone hair serum and dry shampoo buildup, and even sand from the Caribbean Sea that recently got stuck in my hair. It also softens my dry tresses before I even apply conditioner, which is incredible, given how parched my mane is.

Cleansing with Oribe really brings that luxurious feeling of being at the salon’s shampoo bowl from the comfort of my bathroom. Plus, it smells like Calabrian bergamot, white butterfly jasmine, and sandalwood. The blend is so enticing that Oribe even created a perfume inspired by this iconic scent. The chic black bottle pops in my otherwise boring gray bathroom.

And don’t just take my word for it: Foster appreciates that it combines gentle cleansers with conditioning ingredients, such as panthenol, amino acids, proteins, and oils. “It cleanses while still giving the hair a polished, conditioned feel,” she says.

You don’t need to splurge to enjoy a great shampoo, argues Foster. “L’Oréal gives you an elevated experience at the drugstore price point,” she says. “It produces a substantial lather and has more of a fragranced, salon-product feel than many inexpensive shampoos.” She especially likes it for anyone dealing with dryness or color-treated hair, or who wants a gentle daily shampoo without the luxury price tag.

“I love this product. It's available everywhere, which means I can travel light with just hand luggage and pick it up wherever I land,” says celebrity hairstylist and Kennaland salon owner Kenna Kennor. “The results are instantly better than most hotel shampoos.”

A combo of Cécred’s Bioactive keratin ferment and hyaluronic acid gently cleanses my hair while leaving it nourished and detangled, which is not exactly the norm for my dry curls. It works equally well on my natural hair and extensions, and it’s so gentle that you can use it on color-treated hair.

Foster especially likes this one for dry hair because it’s formulated with hydrating ingredients and is sulfate-free. “It is designed to provide slip while cleansing, which is especially helpful for dry, textured or highly manipulated hair,” she says. “If I'm shampooing dry or textured hair and it immediately feels tangled and rough, I know I'm creating more work for myself later. This has a richer, more luxurious lather than people sometimes expect from a hydrating shampoo, and it leaves hair feeling clean without that squeaky, stripped feeling.”

Leave it to tennis star Sloane Stephens to create one of our team’s favorite shampoos. After a sweaty Rumble boxing class, Doc&Glo helped bring that fresh salon feeling to features director Rachel Epstein's shower. The first thing she noticed was the gel-like consistency of the shampoo, which easily lathers in her hands—she only needs two to three pumps. But her favorite part was the calming peppermint-and-eucalyptus scent that lingered for the rest of the night. “None of that fruity garbage over here,” she says.

Epstein has used the shampoo and conditioner twice a week for the last month, and her scalp has consistently felt balanced. Her waves are fresher and fuller the next day. “Because I have dandruff, I still need to use a medicated shampoo here and there, but I’ll definitely continue using this duo,” she says.

Chlorine and hard water can fade your color-treated hair and make neutral and cool tones look warm. This de-brassing shampoo reduces yellowing and brassiness in blonde, highlighted, silver, and gray hair. “I have seen great results with this, and there's no purple buildup,” says Kennor, who especially likes this one for double-process blondes.

Foster appreciates that Virtue isn’t relying solely on heavy purple dye. The tone is actually synthetic color-free and dye-free. De-Brassing Shampoo pairs botanical ingredients with Virtue’s signature Alpha Keratin 60ku protein, a proprietary protein that mimics the hair-strengthening, damage-repairing benefits of keratin.

When you want a splurge-worthy shampoo, opt for this recent Women’s Health Beauty Award winner. “If you color your hair, you need a shampoo that protects your investment,” says beauty director Brian Underwood. “With a sulfate-free formula that ensures your scalp won’t become irritated, this one contains ingredients that soothe, repair, and rejuvenate like grapeseed sterols, chia seed, and hook seaweed.” It also contains a trifecta of quinoa extract, chamomile extract, and amaranth extract to soften, smooth, hydrate, and condition hair.

A bonus: It gently foams up while strengthening and hydrating your highlighted, bleached, or color-treated hair, adds Foster.

K18 is beloved by everyone from Foster and me to the legendary Simone Biles. Peptide Prep is pH-optimized and contains the brand’s signature K18 Peptide along with plant-derived surfactants. “It cleanses without adding stress to already compromised hair,” says Foster. “That's important because damaged hair doesn't need to be babied to the point that it's not being properly cleansed, but it also doesn't need an aggressive shampoo every wash day.” It’s also made with salicylic acid, which gently exfoliates and removes excess scalp oil.

After using this shampoo, I experienced less flaking and less product buildup from heat protectants and scalp oils. My hair feels lighter and bouncier, and I can get away with shampooing once a week instead of twice a week since using this product.

Redken's Acidic Bonding Concentrate is another product Foster likes for chemically processed or damaged hair. “Citric acid is a key component of the formula, designed to help reinforce weakened bonds while maintaining an acidic pH,” she says.

I tried this one during its launch in February and continued using it for several months afterward. My scalp felt so incredibly clean, without that pesky tightness and dryness. When paired with the matching conditioner, I noticed less shedding in my shower. My strands felt more resilient, conditioned, and rebalanced. I also noticed that my hair’s balayage took longer to fade, which is a major win.

Caring for fine hair is tricky because it may need moisture and strengthening but can become flat very quickly if the formula is too rich, says Foster. Ouai contains hydrolyzed keratin, biotin, and chia seed oil to leave your fine hair bouncy without that heavy, overly-conditioned feeling.

This shampoo also suds up in a rich, satisfying way, adding a luxurious touch to the mornings of deputy editor Carina Hsieh. “My hair has more lift at the roots—almost the way it used to, pre-30s,” she says. “My bangs are banging again (physically, emotionally, and, of course, spiritually), and my hair no longer separates into the same three sad little strands it seemed to automatically separate every 2 PM.”

To Hsieh, it only faintly smells of rose and musk. It’s the same fragrance as Ouai’s pet shampoo, but she swears the pet shampoo smells better. “But honestly, that’s me really looking for a negative as I sit and twirl my hair all day,” she says.

“Design Essentials is my absolute favorite shampoo,” says Foster. “The brand has been working with textured hair long before it became a trending topic, and that experience shows with Honey Crème.” This shampoo cleanses while providing slip and helping with detangling. As its name implies, it’s enriched with honey, a moisture-preserving, quick-lathering ingredient that helps soften and smooth the cuticle, says Foster.

You can also use this shampoo if you don’t have curly or coily strands, though you might not need the extra help with detangling. Still, it’s an enjoyable experience at a fantastic price point. “The best shampoo isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It's the one that cleanses your scalp effectively while respecting what your hair needs at that particular time,” says Foster, and Design Essentials proves that with Honey Crème.

I’ve been using Design Essentials since I was in high school. It’s a truly reliable brand that hasn’t compromised on ingredient quality, smell, or feel. My hair is truly softer and more manageable every single time I use this shampoo.

Joico’s Detox Shampoo does just that—it combines a proprietary chelating agent and activated charcoal to remove product buildup and hard-water deposits. This color-safe shampoo also removes trace minerals and salts.

While it’s tough on unwanted components that can compromise my hair's integrity, it also contains moringa seed oil to help prevent dryness. There are also veggie proteins intended to help strengthen weak hair bonds, leaving me with a noticeably cleaner scalp and healthy-looking hair.

Whenever I use this shampoo, my hair feels super clean, but still hydrated. With each wash, my hair is noticeably bouncier, giving me a fresh-from-the-salon look. I also appreciate that this shampoo is compatible with all hair types. My hair is thick and coily, while my mom has fine, color-treated straight hair. This formula worked for both of us, and it has recently become a must-have for her since moving to a new city with hard water.

#4900. Bye-Bye, Beige! This 517-Square-Foot Apartment Became a Creative Retreat Full of Light and Color

“My previous home was dominated by shades of beige,” Jaco Kroon says. “And it no longer suited me.” After a career in marketing, Kroon decided to head in a different direction and devote himself to a new creative pursuit: designing furniture for pets. He found the perfect setting for this fresh start in a 517-square-foot apartment in Amsterdam. Together with Elza Wandler, a designer and founder of her eponymous accessory brand, he created an interior that reflects his evolving vision. “I wanted a place that underscores my new direction—a more colorful, more creative, and more surprising home,” explains Kroon.

A vase by ceramist Pol Chambost brings contrast to the table.

“I’d seen a few articles about Elza Wandler’s home and immediately thought: That’s exactly the kind of environment I want: creative, personal, and full of objects that tell stories,” Kroon recalls. What began as creative interest soon developed into a friendship. During a lunch together in the designer’s garden, the two hit it off right away. In addition to their passion for interior design, they also share a love of dogs—they both own poodles.

As Kroon got to know Wandler’s home better, he was particularly struck by the fact that every object had its own unique character. They wanted to create a similar atmosphere in his apartment, which led to a close creative collaboration in which they both contributed their ideas and visions. For Kroon, his home soon became more than just a place to live: “While the work was underway, I was developing my own line of pet furniture and realized just how much the new interior was influencing my creative work as well.”

Jaco Kroon’s love for animals has come to shape his career. He’s seen here with his faithful toy poodle, Elio.

The biggest challenge of the project was making the best use of the limited space. The 517-square-foot apartment combines a kitchen, living room, dining area, and sleeping area without feeling cramped or having to make any sacrifices. According to Wandler, the key was to view the spaces as a cohesive ecosystem: “In such small spaces, every single object interacts with the others. Even a four-inch-tall vase can completely alter the balance of a room.”

The bedroom is decorated in shades of salmon, with custom cabinets framing the bed. The wallpaper is by Kelly Wearstler. Wall sconces by Contain and the bedding is by Bonsoirs.

This gave rise to the project’s motto: “Every item must be a Beyoncé”—that’s how Wandler and Kroon jokingly describe their design philosophy. It’s their way of expressing the idea that every piece should bring its own personality and presence to the home without disrupting the harmony of the environment. The color scheme also follows this principle with intense yet carefully coordinated tones—such as the eggplant in the kitchen and the warm, velvety salmon pink in the bedroom—paired with textured woods, vintage fabrics, and custom details. “At first, the idea of a burgundy-violet kitchen really put me off,” Kroon admits with a smile. “But the further we got into the project, the more I felt my horizons expanding.”

A blue bowl by Wandler x SolidNature and a ceramic basket by Ferm Living add splashes of color to the burgundy kitchen. The art on the wall is by Laura de Wilde.

One distinctive feature of the project is the interplay between functionality and aesthetics: Practical solutions blend so naturally into the design that they are barely recognizable as such at first glance. The historic Amsterdam townhouse, with its large windows, had very little storage space. That’s why Wandler took advantage of nearly every opportunity to create additional storage solutions. Custom cabinets frame the bed like an architectural backdrop, while the TV disappears into a specially designed piece of furniture made of zebrawood.

“Elza has turned what would normally be a purely functional piece of furniture into something beautiful. She even convinced me to hide the TV behind the doors of a zebrawood cabinet!” jokes Kroon. “Everything seems to have been designed for aesthetic reasons, but in fact, every element is tailored to make optimal use of the available space.” The decision to use zebrawood also follows this philosophy: Its striking grain lends the interior a vertical dynamism and makes the room appear more spacious. “I wanted to use the wood to create movement and depth,” explains Wandler. “In a small room, you always have to consider how to increase the sense of space.”

Colorful accents, such as the stool by Rutger de Regt, make a bold statement in the interior. The vase is by India Mahdavi and the sculpture on the wall is by Floor Merjenburgh.

As is often the case with Wandler’s projects, restored vintage pieces, contemporary design, and works by young artists all find a place side by side here. The large vintage sofa was completely reupholstered, while the artwork and decorative pieces come from a network of emerging designers and artists supported by the designer through Kamer—her curatorial platform dedicated to collectible design.

The dark wood of the floor complements the chocolate-brown armchair by Norr11.

“It’s important to me that I feel happy in my home,” says Kroon. “And that it stimulates creativity.” Wandler sought to create this feeling through her selection of artwork and a carefully coordinated lighting design. The latter plays a central role in the living concept: Since the apartment faces multiple directions, the natural light changes constantly throughout the day, causing colors and materials to appear different depending on the time. This creates the impression that this small apartment was conceived as a place that evolves and can accompany personal transformation; it embraces new ideas, new ambitions, and new identities. “The greatest compliment,” Wandler concludes, “was when Jaco said to me, ‘Now I feel like I’m finally living as the version of myself that I want to become.’”

The dining area, with a table from Westwing, is connected to the living room. The vintage sofa by Cini Boeri for Arflex has been reupholstered; the vase in front of the window is by l’Objet.

#4899. Bitcoin falls below $60K for first time since July amid broader market selloff

Bitcoin fell nearly 6% as US stocks declined, with the Nasdaq dropping more than 2% and Anthropic shares losing almost 10%.

Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since July, extending its recent losses amid a broader selloff in technology stocks and other risk assets.

Bitcoin (BTC) had fallen to $58,811 before recovering slightly to trade around $59,503, down 5.6% over the past 24 hours as of 16:52 UTC on Friday, according to CoinGecko data. The cryptocurrency has fallen 13.8% over the past week and nearly 30% over the past month.

The decline came amid a broader selloff in US equities. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.28% at 22,617.73, while the S&P 500 fell 3.69% to 6,910.77 on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance.

Shares of Anthropic (ANT), which made its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, closed down 8.50% at $88.91 amid concerns over valuations and spending in the artificial intelligence sector.

US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded $582.3 million in net outflows on Thursday, up from $306.5 million the previous day, according to Farside Investors. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals.

Bitcoin’s decline appears to be driven more by the broader selloff in artificial intelligence stocks than by problems specific to the cryptocurrency market, according to James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares.

Butterfill told Cointelegraph that Bitcoin has increasingly traded alongside other liquidity-sensitive growth assets, with deteriorating sentiment toward AI stocks spilling into crypto as investors reduce risk. The prospect of interest rates remaining elevated has made the broader selloff more severe, he added.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, following a quarter-point increase in September. Traders on Polymarket were pricing in a 94% chance of another rate hike by the Fed’s next policy decision on Dec. 9, as of 17:19 UTC on Friday.

Polymarket traders price in 94% chance of another Fed rate hike in 2026. Source: Polymarket

Despite Bitcoin falling below $60,000, Butterfill said the decline has not fundamentally changed his medium-term outlook.

Butterfill said Bitcoin could face further short-term losses if the AI selloff deepens, but should benefit relatively quickly if technology stocks stabilize.

Alexander Blume, founder and CEO of digital asset investment firm Two Prime, told Cointelegraph that macroeconomic instability, interest rates, inflation and a lack of Bitcoin-specific catalysts were contributing to the decline.

However, Blume suggested that selling pressure may be nearing an end.

#4898. The 10 Best Walking Shoes for Men, According to Men’s Health Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our experts recommend shoes from Hoka and Asics.

What can motivate you to get out for a few extra weekly walks? A pair of ultra-comfortable walking shoes that keep your feet happy long after you've reached your target.

"All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J. Mendeszoon, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon.

"Wear the same socks you wear when you walk when trying them on and remember that our feet expand while walking."

Once you find the right pair, keep in mind to replace them after you've racked up some miles. "It is important to realize that shoes are generally good for 500 to 600 miles," says Mendeszoon.
