If your walking routine takes you through city streets, sidewalks, or even the gym, the On Cloud X4 is built to keep pace with style. This newest version of On’s beloved crossover trainer retains its signature featherweight feel but adds key comfort upgrades that make it better suited for all-day wear. The breathable mesh upper stays cool and flexible, while plusher materials around the heel and tongue provide a more dialed-in, cushioned fit than the X3.

The real update lies in the underfoot tech: the Hellion superfoam midsole delivers soft landings, and the X-shaped Speedboard adds forefoot flex and energy return, whether you're walking forward or moving side to side. A midfoot cage adds extra structure, while a grippy rubber outsole gives you confident traction on pavement or polished floors.

This is still a firmer-feeling shoe, so don’t expect the plushness of a max-cushion trainer, but the Cloudtec pods adapt nicely to your stride and deliver a responsive feel that’s great for quick city walks or active errands.

This newest version of the Glycerin, the Glycerin 22, leans into what the series does best: plush comfort and a dialed-in neutral fit. The nitrogen-infused midsole foam has been fine-tuned for even better softness and smoother transitions, making it ideal for long walks when comfort is a top priority.

Unlike traditional stability shoes, the Glycerin 22 doesn’t use any rigid support posts. Instead, it relies on a wider platform and balanced midfoot geometry to provide a naturally stable base without feeling corrective. The result is a super-soft, highly neutral ride that feels consistent from heel strike to toe-off, whether you have 2 miles or 12 miles ahead of you.

The upper remains breathable and accommodating, and the shoe's durable outsole is built to handle high weekly mileage without wearing down quickly. It’s not flashy, but it’s reliable, and that’s exactly why people keep coming back to it.

It's worth noting that the Brooks Glycerin 23 was recently released, with minor design updates that make it a heavier yet more cushioned shoe. Personally, I prefer the lighter version, and with the price drop, the 22 is a great value.

If you’re looking for a reliable walking shoe that won’t wreck your budget, the Asics Gel-Pulse 17 builds on the success of the 15 with a few key upgrades to comfort and breathability. The FF BLAST midsole and signature GEL cushioning are still here. Meaning you get a soft, responsive ride whether you’re walking city blocks or putting in time on the treadmill. What’s new is the jacquard mesh upper, which offers a lighter, more ventilated feel than last year’s engineered mesh. It helps your feet breathe better on warm days or longer walks without compromising the structure you need for all-day support.

One standout design feature is the elevated midsole through the center, which enhances support and impact absorption across key pressure points. While the foam leans on the firmer side, the added GEL insert softens landings, making it a strong pick for steady-paced daily walks. Stability gets a boost too—thanks to strategic bumpers along the heel that cradle the foot, paired with a rigid heel counter that helps limit excess movement.

If you liked the 16, this one feels like a natural upgrade—just a bit cooler and more dialed in for summer.

The Kuru Atom 2 is designed as a comfort-focused athletic shoe that blends performance features with orthopedic support, making it also one of the best new shoes for stability on the market. The minimalistic style behind the shoe appeals to me, especially when opting for the white or black colorways. I’ll also say that I was impressed at how easily the shoe slipped on, which is a bit of a non-negotiable for me unless I’m doing a trail run or putting in a lot of miles.

The first thing I noticed was how comfortable the shoe was, with its cushioned midsole and KURUSOLE heel shock absorption still providing a solidly responsive ride. This makes it a perfect pick for anyone looking for a daily trainer for low mileage or full days of walking. The Atom 2 offers a moderate improvement over the shoe’s previous energy return, but it still isn’t a running shoe you want to hit the pavement with for long distances.

The Kuru Atom 2 is a little heavy on the foot, which comes from the stability and durability that it provides. And thanks to the clean aesthetic, it fits in almost any setting, from the track to the grocery store.

The Brooks Ghost 17 proves why this Seattle-based brand remains a household name in performance footwear. Founded in 1914, Brooks has built its reputation on reliability, comfort, and a no-frills design approach—and the Ghost line is the perfect example of that. While the brand has recently taken steps to modernize its look and appeal to a younger generation, the Ghost 17 still leans traditional in the best way: It’s well-cushioned, durable, and consistent from mile one to mile 100.

The Brooks Ghost has long been a go-to for runners and walkers alike—and the Ghost 17 kept that reputation alive with subtle but smart upgrades. This version uses an air mesh upper for breathability, along with a redesigned kickback collar that cradles the heel without rubbing or slipping. The biggest change from the Ghost 16, though, is underfoot: Brooks added nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and forefoot, giving the shoe a softer, more cushioned feel than previous versions. We should note that the Ghost 18 just released, and while we’re still in the early stages of testing it, it still uses that DNA Loft v3 foam but gets a fully rebuilt upper and tongue.

What makes the Ghost 17 such a standout is its adaptability. Whether you're on your feet for hours, squeezing in a quick power walk, or just want something that holds up across daily mileage, this is an easy choice. It’s not flashy—but that’s kind of the point. It’s durable, balanced, and built for comfort, making it an ideal “one-shoe-fits-most” option. And with the Ghost 18 just releasing, the price drop on the 17 still makes it worthwhile.

Asics has refined the Gel-Nimbus line year after year, and the twenty-eighth iteration is one of its most luxurious yet. Known for max cushioning and long-wear comfort, this model upgrades the upper with a premium, breathable knit that feels as good as it performs. The toe box is also more spacious than in previous versions. A welcome relief for walkers who often feel squeezed in standard neutral shoes.

Underfoot, the Gel-Nimbus 28 still delivers a soft and stable ride, thanks to its combo of lightweight foam and added gel (FF Blast Plus ECO) cushioning in the forefoot and heel. The 8mm drop subtly rolls the foot forward, creating that ideal balance between protection and propulsion. The flexible knit tongue and solid heel lockdown add to the premium feel, making it a go-to for long walks, recovery days, or even light runs.

Men's Health Deputy Editor Paul Kita enjoyed how they felt structured, but not restrictive. Plus, Asics beefed up the outsole for better traction and longer wear. This pair will keep pace with more use. And while it's built for a neutral gait, it plays nicely with custom insoles if you need more arch support or pronation control.

Two defining features set Altra shoes apart: a roomy toe box and a zero-drop platform. This combination ensures an anatomic fit and promotes a natural gait. Your feet enjoy greater freedom to move naturally, allowing your toes to flex and bend as you walk, which encourages better biomechanics and can reduce strain on your foot's structures.

Compared to other Altras, the Via Olympus 2 leans more toward plush than performance. The wide-base footbed adds stability, while the rocker-shaped sole still promotes a smooth forward roll with each step—even if it’s more subtle during walking than running. That extra room in the toe box and midfoot also comes in handy during longer efforts, giving your foot space to swell without feeling cramped.

"I love super high stack shoes like this, and Altra’s dedication to extra-roomy toe boxes makes the Via Olympus 2 even more comfortable," notes Williams. "The rocker shape is less pronounced on my walks than when I run in them, but it’s still noticeable for turnover on each step."

If you're planning long walks, you'll appreciate how the shoe's roomy toe box accommodates the natural expansion that occurs during extended physical activity.

Fashion meets function with this shoe. It showcases a stylish design while seamlessly integrating waterproof features, exceptional durability, and a rocker bottom that ensures a buttery-smooth walking experience. It not only performs well, but looks good doing it.

It's explicitly designed for outdoor activities, making it an ideal choice for those who do most of their walking in nature. Thanks to its waterproof properties, my feet stay snug and dry, even in challenging weather conditions. Whether I'm trudging through rain-soaked paths or navigating puddles, these shoes provide unwavering protection for my feet.

Let's talk about Keen's newly patented "constant curve" construction. This design is engineered to encourage forward momentum in the wearer's stride, similar to most Hoka models. The rocker bottom facilitates a smooth transition from heel strike to toe-off, which Keen hopes can make walking more enjoyable for wearers. Based on my personal experience with these shoes, I'd say Keen has succeeded. I find myself walking faster and expending less effort, especially during long or uphill treks.

Although some reviewers have noted a rubbery off-gassing scent when the shoes are fresh out of the box, I didn't find it particularly noticeable (and I'm pretty sensitive to smells).

The Kuru Atom Trail is a purpose-built trail walking shoe designed to protect your heels, support your stride, and keep you moving confidently over rough ground. Its standout feature is the brand’s proprietary Kuru Sole, a dynamic midsole system that flexes with each step to cup and cradle the heel. Compared to traditional heel cradles, this one offers more adaptability and a locked-in feel. This is especially helpful for walkers who deal with heel pain or plantar fasciitis.

On the trail, the Atom Trail holds its own. A synthetic upper with rugged TPU overlays adds structure and durability, while the gusseted tongue helps block out debris. The outsole is aggressive and grippy, built for varied surfaces. It’s not the lightest or most responsive option out there. Which is why we wouldn’t recommend it for trail running but rather for long hikes, uneven terrain, and daily dog walks on gravel or dirt paths; it’s an excellent pick.

Mendeszoon puts it best: "This is a true traditional trail shoe that provides great support, comfort, and protection against the elements and uneven and challenging terrain." Our only qualm is that it's a little heavy and not particularly responsive, which is why we wouldn't recommend running it. But it excels in what it's meant for—trail walking.

Bonus points: it’s made with fully vegan materials and has enough breathability to handle summer hikes without overheating your feet.

Look for walking shoes with support and stability features labeled for your specific foot type. "Consider your foot type and [walking] gait," says Dr. Bradley Schaeffer, DPM. "The goal is to keep your lower body in alignment as much as possible." Features such as a firm heel counter, a supportive midsole, and a secure lacing system can provide the stability you need for comfortable walking and to keep your feet properly aligned.

When it comes to classification, if the shoe is stable, it is designed to help offset pronation, which is the inward rolling of the feet after landing on the ground. When a shoe is neutral, it lacks the stabilizing features, allowing your foot to fall more naturally. When a shoe is moderate, it is somewhere between those two worlds.

"Cushioning absorbs shock and helps to avoid tissue irritation and damage," explains Schaeffer. It's important to choose walking shoes with sufficient cushioning to absorb impact and shock with each step. Look for shoes with cushioned insoles and midsoles made from materials like foam or gel to ensure a comfortable walking experience, especially for longer walks or on hard surfaces.

Decide if you prefer soft cushioning for impact absorption and comfort or a more responsive feel. Some shoes offer a balance between the two, so choose based on your preferences and walking style.

If you're in the market for a walking shoe to take you long distances frequently, be sure the models you're considering are relatively lightweight. Unless we're talking about a stability or trail shoe, which feature additional materials for added durability and support, that means under 11 ounces.

Pay attention to the upper material of the walking shoes, as it can impact comfort, breathability, and durability. Opt for shoes with breathable and flexible uppers made from materials like mesh or knit fabric to help keep your feet cool and comfortable. Additionally, keep an eye out for features like padded collars and tongues for even more comfort and support.

I’m a certified strength and conditioning specialist based in New York and a fitness writer who loves trying the latest gear and raving to my loved ones about his latest discoveries. I have a dog, and I take him for walks twice a day. I also trek through the city from Queens to Manhattan five to six times per week. I have a pretty full roster of clients that I see in-person for training sessions and hit about 15,000 to 20,000 steps per day. Needless to say, I am on my feet A LOT, so I need to be on top of my game when it comes to comfy footwear.

I also got some assistance from Men’s Health fitness editors and medical advisors. We spent months of testing and researching to create this guide. Over the past few years, we’ve logged miles in more than 40 pairs of walking and running shoes from top brands like Asics, Hoka, Brooks, On, and more. Led by Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM and Fitness Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, along with expert input from podiatrists Schaeffer and Mendeszoon, we evaluated each shoe for fit, comfort, cushioning, support, durability, and value. We also considered real-world feedback from testers who wore these shoes during daily walks, commutes, and all-day wear.

From minimalist trainers to max-cushioned picks, we curated this list to meet a variety of foot types, walking styles, and comfort preferences—so you can find the pair that’s right for your stride.

Understanding your foot type is essential for finding the right walking shoes that offer optimal comfort and support. There are three primary arch types based on arch height: neutral, high, and flat. To determine your arch type, you can start with a simple "wet test," Mendeszoon recommends. Wet your feet and stand on a surface like concrete, sand, or a flattened paper bag. Examine the imprint left by your foot.

If your foot leaves a complete, flat imprint, you likely have low arches and would benefit from arch support or stability shoes. If the imprint shows the heel, outer side of the foot, ball of the foot, and toes, but not the arch, you might have a neutral or high arch.

While the wet test provides a basic idea, factors such as weight, biomechanics, and overall fitness also help determine your arch type accurately. For a more detailed analysis, consider visiting a local chiropractic clinic, podiatry practice, or high-quality running shoe store. Some locations offer foot scans that provide intricate information about your feet and arches.

Todd Sinett from Tru Whole Care in New York highlights a special machine called the Foot Levelers Digital Foot Scanner, which identifies specific pressure points on your feet that could be linked to back pain. This advanced tool offers precise measurements for customized orthotics, ensuring tailored support for your unique foot structure.

Yes, running shoes can absolutely be worn for walking, according to Mendeszoon. In fact, they may offer some added benefit compared to conventional walking shoes.

Running shoes are designed to absorb the impact of running, which means they can also provide good shock absorption when walking. Many people choose to wear running shoes for walking because of added support and flexibility, too.

One downside: Running shoes tend to be heavier and less breathable than walking shoes because of their more durable design. So, it's important to note that they may not be the best choice for long-distance walking.

It's important to replace your walking shoes regularly to ensure adequate support and cushioning, probably more frequently than you think. As a general rule of thumb, it's recommended to replace walking shoes every 300 to 500 miles (or every 3 to 5 months for those who walk for at least 45 minutes at least 3 times per week).

The specific lifespan of a shoe depends on several factors, including the frequency and intensity of use, the shoe's quality, and the type of surface you typically walk on. There are a few signs to look out for that may indicate it's time to replace your shoes:

Ultimately, it's important to listen to your body and pay attention to any signs of discomfort or pain when walking. If you notice any of the above signs, it's a good idea to start looking for a new pair of walking shoes.

Powerlifting legend Mark Bell is a huge fan of walking for weight loss, as is Will Smith. This guy lost 60 pounds with walking and bodyweight workouts. And this guy lost 200 pounds by walking and eating a CICO diet. It's all about starting to add to your daily step count, and really sticking with it.

"Starting slow and working your way up is better than overdoing it and giving up," Chris Gagliardi, a certified personal trainer at the American Council on Exercise, previously told Men's Health. An easy way to approach it: Commit to a quick 10-minute walk after dinner, and gradually increase the duration as you become more comfortable with daily movement.

Step counting also helps. "If you’re only getting 3,000 steps on a typical day, don’t try to get 10,000 steps the next day. That can be really discouraging. Aim for 5,000 every day for a week. Then go up to 7,000 the next week," walking coach Michele Stanten, founder of MyWalkingCoach.com and author of The Walking Solution, previously told Men's Health.

Eric Sung, CSCS, is a New York City–based trainer and a member of MH’s Strength in Diversity Initiative.He specializes in athletic training and recently completed his first triathlon.

Dr Mark Mendeszoon is a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon at Precision Orthopaedic Specialties in Chardon, Ohio and owner of Achilles Running Shops in Willoughby , Ohio and Erie, Pa. He  still enjoys working out, running  and coaching runners of all ages.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

The couple reveal their hidden skills during a round of “In Fitness and In Health.”

#4896. Sky Protocol sees $2 billion in stablecoin withdrawals, disputes illicit fund claims

Sky says its USDS stablecoin held its $1 value despite more than $2 billion in withdrawals, as it disputes a report linking the protocol to illicit activity.

Sky Protocol processed more than $2 billion in stablecoin redemptions on Thursday, the same day a CoinDesk investigation linked $518 million in transactions through the protocol to illicit activity.

The withdrawals involved users exchanging Sky’s USDS stablecoin for Circle’s USDC through its Peg Stability Module (PSM), a system that allows users to swap the tokens at a fixed rate.

Sky, which has a total value locked (TVL) of $2.3 billion, said on Friday in a statement that USDS maintained its $1 peg throughout the withdrawals. According to the protocol, the amount of USDC held in the PSM never fell below $800 million and had climbed back above $1.1 billion by Friday.

Sky also challenged the investigation, pointing to a review by Block Analitica, which notably serves as a risk adviser to the Sky ecosystem.

The withdrawals came amid concerns raised by the investigation that Circle could freeze USDC held by Sky, potentially making it harder for users to redeem their stablecoins.

CoinDesk’s Nov. 19 report looked at research by blockchain analytics firm Inca Digital, which identified $518 million in transactions involving wallets linked to hackers, sanctioned entities, and other threat actors over a span of five years.

Of that amount, around $101.9 million was linked to North Korean actors, including wallets connected to the February 2025 Bybit hack.

Meanwhile, Block Analitica disputed some parts of the investigation, saying that the $518 million represented less than 0.06% of the more than $960 billion processed through Sky’s peg stability modules.

The firm said about two-thirds of the flagged activity occurred between 2021 and mid-2024 – before Sky introduced its newer LitePSM system.

Block Analitica also questioned the reported links to North Korean threat actors, stating that some wallets were several transactions removed from known addresses and may have belonged to unrelated users.

The firm added that most of the flagged transactions passed through trading services such as 1inch, ParaSwap and MetaMask Swaps, which automatically choose where to route trades.

The large withdrawals also came amid a sharp drop in the number of USDS tokens in circulation. The supply fell nearly 40% in one day to about 3.2 billion tokens, according to DefiLlama data. However, the stablecoin maintained its $1 value despite the decline.

CoinDesk reported that a wallet linked to crypto exchange Poloniex accounted for a large share of the withdrawals, although it wasn’t clear whether the exchange itself was behind the transactions.

The combined circulating supply of Sky’s USDS and DAI stablecoins fell to $6.11 billion as of Nov. 20, down 37.8% over the past 30 days. Source: Sky Ecosystem Financial Insights

Sky said it held about $9.3 billion in assets backing its stablecoins as of Friday, compared with around $6.11 billion in USDS and DAI in circulation, according to its financial dashboard. The dashboard also showed about $93 million in reserves to help cover potential losses.

Cointelegraph reached out to the Sky Frontier Foundation for comment but had not received a response by publication.

#4895. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4894. Elvis Presley at Home: Tour the King’s Private Life in 14 Photos, From the Heartland to Hawaii

Elvis Presley is one of those icons so permanently etched into the fabric of American popular culture that it seems, nearly half a century after his death, as if he will live forever. While Presley also had homes in California, and famously lived in Germany during his stint in the US Army, it is Graceland that is most strongly associated with the late musician. The rock and roller’s Memphis residence where he lived for 20 years and where he died at the age of 42, Graceland is America’s second-most-visited residence, behind the White House. Every year, an average of 600,000 people flock to the residence turned museum, which opened to the public in 1982.

Today, the museum, which encompasses Presley’s gravesite, former home, and a collection of mementos of Presley’s rock-and-roll career, stands as a stirring reminder of one man’s life, as he grew from a beloved child to poverty-stricken parents to, arguably, the most famous man in the world. Below, we’re rounding up photos of the legendary musician at his (almost) equally famous home, and other places he rested his pompadoured head.

The Presleys at home in Tupelo, around 1945

Presley and his parents pose for a photo at home in Tupelo, Mississippi, circa 1945—the year before he received his first guitar. The future king of rock and roll was born nearby, in a two-room house built by his father, grandfather, and uncle on January 8, 1935. That house, now a museum, was repossessed three years later, and the family bounced around other homes in the area before moving to Memphis when Presley was 13 years old. There, the family lived in Lauderdale Courts, a public housing project.

In March 1956, riding high on the success of Presley’s first RCA single, “Heartbreak Hotel,” the family became homeowners for the very first time. A house of her own had always been Gladys’s dream, and her 21-year-old son made it a reality when he paid $29,250 for 1034 Audubon Drive, a low-rise, seven-room ranch house with four bedrooms. Gladys likened it to living in a palace. They also added a backyard pool–at the time, it was the only one on the street. While most wealthy men of his tender age might have set their parents up with a house before shimmying off to live the bachelor’s life elsewhere, this wasn’t Elvis’s style; living together as a close-knit trio was always part of his master plan.

Elvis Presley and a friend chat in the back yard of his house at 1034 Audubon Drive in 1956.

On their quiet, leafy street in the rapidly growing East Memphis, the Presleys were soon living the suburban dream. Things might well have stayed that way too, had Elvis’s star not reached stratospheric heights over the following months. By the summer of 1956, Elvis had recorded smash hits “Hound Dog” and “Don’t Be Cruel.” His first feature film, Love Me Tender, premiered later that year, making him a bona fide movie star.

Elvis and his parents relax on the patio.

Elvis kicks his feet up alongside his parents on the Audubon Drive home’s patio in this July 1956 photo. The Presleys had moved to this upper-middle-class neighborhood just four months prior. During their residency, the family tried to fit in with their neighbors in the affluent community to the best of their ability; Gladys let local kids cool off in their newly installed pool and made them peanut butter sandwiches, while Elvis would take them for a spin on the back of his gleaming motorcycle. But it soon became clear that Elvis’s fame would put a strain on life in the area. Perhaps it was when Hollywood star Natalie Wood came to stay at the house on Audubon—which turned the street into a circus as fans gathered to watch her pose outside on Elvis’s motorcycle—or the hot dog stand that set up outside that magically appeared to feed the constant stream of fans. The final straw may have been when a helicopter landed on the vacant lot beside the house to collect Elvis, leaving the neighbors well and truly shaken up.

By March 1957 the Presleys had packed their bags and moved on from the house on Audubon, restoring a relative sense of peace to the quaint suburban neighborhood. The family may have spent just a year at their Audubon Drive home, but it was a pivotal chapter in Elvis’s life story, marking a transition between the transient lifestyle of his impoverished childhood and the security and permanence he would find in his next home: Graceland.

The new homeowner with his hand on one of Graceland’s now iconic columns.

Presley skyrocketed to stardom in the mid ’50s, garnering a recording contract with RCA Records. This newfound wealth meant the boy whose home was repossessed, and who lived in public housing, could now buy the lavish house of his dreams for himself and his parents. In March 1957, the 22-year-old “Hound Dog” singer paid $102,500 for Graceland, which would remain his primary residence for the rest of his life. The home had been built in 1939 on a plot of land the original owner named after his daughter, Grace; the name stuck. Here, Presley leans on one of the home’s pillars shortly after the purchase.

Elvis in wrought iron, and in the flesh, at the gates to Graceland.

The musician poses in front of Graceland’s famous wrought iron music note gate in April 1957, around the time he had it installed. Abe Saucer designed the gates—which feature life-size images of Elvis playing guitar amid musical notes—and had them custom-built by John Dillars Jr. At the time, the property spanned 13.8 acres, with the mansion clocking in at over 10,200 square feet—later, Elvis would expand it to 17,500 square feet and 23 rooms, with additions including the famous Jungle Room.

A palace fit for the king of rock and roll.

The “Burning Love” singer walks in front of Graceland, circa 1957. Early design details that Presley added to the Colonial Revival estate included a custom 15-foot-long blue metallic sofa (later reupholstered in white), a pink flagstone wall around the property, a kidney-shaped swimming pool, and a full-size soda fountain. In his initial renovations, Presley spent $500,000 (over $5 million in today’s dollars).

In March 1958, Presley was drafted into the US Army. He is pictured in his off-post home in Bad Nauheim, Germany, in January 1960, shortly after being promoted to sergeant. It was here that the 24-year-old singer met a 14-year-old Priscilla Beaulieu, when a friend of his who had spotted Priscilla at a restaurant brought her to a party at Presley’s place to introduce them. To this day, the home at 14 Goethestrasse is still a landmark for fans.

Elvis and his father mourning after the death of Gladys.

Elvis and his father Vernon on the steps of Graceland in August 1958, shortly after the deathof his beloved mother, Gladys. The two had been exceptionally close, and her loss was toprove a devastating turning point. Elvis had always believed that the purpose of his extraordinary success was to provide his parents with the security and comfort they had been denied during his childhood. Buying them a home, and ultimately one as grand as Graceland, had been central to that vision. But now, just as he had achieved everything he had worked for, his mother was gone. With the loss of her unwavering love and support, it was as though a curtain had fallen on Elvis’s life. The young man who had once seemed so certain of his place in the world would never quite be the same again.

In March, 1960, Presley was discharged from the Army and returned home to Graceland, but it was a sadder and lonelier place, since Gladys died while he was in basic training. Here, he stands with his Rolls-Royce in front of Graceland, circa 1960. The Jailhouse Rock star had an affinity for slick cars, but it wasn’t the only mode of transportation he enjoyed at the estate. Priscilla Beaulieu, who came to visit him at Graceland in 1962 and moved in the following year, wrote in her 1985 memoir Elvis and Me that he “turned Graceland into a private playground for us all. He’d have gun-shooting contests and also ‘screaming thrill rides’ when he’d pack several people into his custom-built golf cart and race around the grounds at top speed.”

Elvis and Priscilla were married in Las Vegas on May 1, 1967. He was 32; she was 21. Exactly nine months later, on February 1, 1968, their first and only child, Lisa Marie Presley, was born

Priscilla and Elvis brought a tropical design aesthetic home from their vacations in Hawaii.

Hawaii became a bit of a home away from home for Presley following his 1961 film, Blue Hawaii. He returned often to vacation there, including in 1968, when this snapshot was taken. The “Don’t Be Cruel” singer was so inspired by the tropical locale that he added a tiki-inspired space to Graceland. Now known as the Jungle Room, the kitschy den features wood-paneled walls, green shag carpeting on the floor and ceiling, carved wooden furniture with faux fur upholstery, and a built-in rock waterfall feature.

Priscilla, Elvis, and baby Lisa Marie relax at home.

The Presleys relax in Graceland’s pool area, circa 1970. He had added the kidney-shaped pool and flagstone patio to the property in 1957. This snapshot shares a relaxed, happy moment, but life with Elvis wasn’t all pool parties for Priscilla. In Elvis and Me, Priscilla wrote frankly about their controversial relationship: “When we met, I had just turned 14. The first six months I spent with him were filled with tenderness and affection. Blinded by love, I saw none of his faults or weaknesses. He was to become the passion of my life. He taught me everything: how to dress, how to walk, how to apply makeup and wear my hair, how to behave, how to return love—his way. Over the years he became my father, husband, and very nearly God.”

Elvis and Lisa Marie are shown here on the porch of Graceland in the early 1970s. Lisa Marie later recalled the curious rhythms of life at the mansion. Her father was nocturnal, she explained, and the household rarely got going before about two in the afternoon. Lisa Marie remembered fondly hearing the rotary phone ring and being summoned upstairs to spend quality time with her dad in his bedroom. “I would just sit up there, and he’d talk to me and ask what I was doing while he watched one of his 17 televisions or listened to records,” she said in her memoir, From Here to the Great Unknown, co-written with her daughter Riley Keough. On occasion, Elvis would come downstairs and take the family and their friends out for an impromptu evening at the movie theater, shutting it down so they could watch a James Bond film or The Pink Panther.

#4893. Wrapped Monero token crashes 99.8% amid suspected $13.5M exploit

Bitquery traced $13.5 million in suspicious sales of the wrapped Monero token, as its operator blamed a security breach and promised to reimburse affected traders.

A wrapped version of Monero (XMR) plunged more than 99% on Hyperliquid on Friday after a wallet that received tokens from the deployer account sold approximately $13.5 million worth of the asset, according to blockchain analytics firm Bitquery.

The token, known as XMR1, fell from around $500 to $1 in roughly 30 minutes, a 99.8% decline, according to Bitquery. Wrapped tokens are designed to represent other cryptocurrencies on different blockchains, allowing them to be traded outside their native networks. The collapse affected XMR1 rather than Monero’s native cryptocurrency.

According to Bitquery’s onchain analysis, the wallet received 5.2 million XMR1 tokens from the deployer account before selling approximately $13.5 million worth of the asset on Friday.

The firm traced $13.28 million in USDC transferred to Arbitrum, where $13.22 million was exchanged for 7,467 Ether (ETH) through CoW Protocol. Most of the ETH was subsequently bridged to Ethereum.

Bitquery also found that proceeds from four hacks earlier in November, involving Across Protocol, Kava, Lighter and Safe, had been used to purchase approximately $6.6 million worth of XMR1, apparently as a route to native Monero. The firm said it found no onchain evidence linking those incidents to Friday’s suspected exploit.

Value of XMR1 purchases linked to funds from four November hacks. Source: Bitquery

Bitquery said its onchain investigation could not establish how the deployer account’s private key was obtained or who controlled it during the transfers, leaving the circumstances of the suspected compromise unconfirmed.

Related: Binance hacker moves nearly $600M in ETH, routes funds through THORChain, Chainflip

PerpetualCow, the pseudonymous operator of Wagyu, the service behind XMR1, attributed the collapse to an alleged breach of hosting provider 1984, claiming that customer data and internal server files had been exposed.

According to PerpetualCow, the XMR1 deployer key had been stored on a server that was subsequently deleted, but the hosting provider allegedly retained logs and files associated with it.

PerpetualCow also pledged to personally reimburse affected traders and said Wagyu would relaunch at a later date, although no timeline was provided.

Cointelegraph contacted the operator for additional details about the suspected breach and reimbursement plans but had not received a response by publication.

#4892. The 8 Best Home Office Chairs, Approved by Spine Specialists

The best seats for boosting productivity and evading back pain.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you work from home, you know how much of a difference the right office chair can make. Take it from someone who's spent five years working remotely and learned the hard way that the couch isn't the best place to spend a workday. Between a standing desk, an under-desk treadmill, and monitors, outfitting your home office can get expensive. But if you're going to splurge on one piece of WFH gear, an ergonomic office chair that supports your back throughout the workday is a good place to start.

“A supportive chair can reduce the risk of lower back pain, neck and upper back pain, poor circulation, and fatigue,” says Kevin Lees, director of chiropractic operations at The Joint Chiropractic. “This may also lead to improved productivity, enabling individuals to stay focused on their tasks without distractions from trying to get comfortable.”

To find the best home office chairs, our team consulted spine specialists and tested several popular ergonomic chairs for weeks in our own workspaces, sitting for up to eight hours a day. Our favorite is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, which impressed us with its customizable support and easy assembly at a reasonable price compared to premium models from Herman Miller and Steelcase.

The right home office chair will be different for everyone, but there are a lot of factors that will remain the same, like adjustable lumbar support and thick seat cushioning. Keep reading to find which of these eight expert-recommended chairs are the perfect addition to your workday.

Meet the experts: Kevin Lees, Director of Chiropractic Operations at The Joint Chiropractic.Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care.

The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our pick for the best home office chair because of its combination of comfort, adjustability, and value. At $499, it’s packed with easy-to-use adjustments that make it a steal. You can customize the seat depth, lumbar support, tilt tension, recline, and more without having to take your eyes away from your work.

After testing the chair for over a month and sitting for four to six hours per workday, WH Digital Designer Taryn Colbert gave it a five out of five, praising how easy it was to assemble and customize. In fact, she found herself using it even when she wasn't working.

“While I work, I sit it up to work on my posture,” she says. When doing her hair or playing computer games, she reclines the chair into what she calls “lounge mode.”

The armrests alone offer five types of adjustment, and you can add a headrest or a taller cylinder for an additional cost. While the mesh version has a low-key look, the leather and vegan leather options are worth considering if you want a bit more style.

Colbert’s biggest gripe was the wide wheelbase, which made it difficult to maneuver through doorways and across carpet.

Still, if you’re looking for a classic ergonomic office chair, this model is great for both first-timers and seasoned remote workers. Its customizable design is intuitive enough to use every day without requiring a four-figure investment.

From the iconic Eames Lounge Chair to the ergonomic Aeron office chair, Herman Miller has earned its reputation for making some of the best seats around. At upwards of $1,500, the Aeron is certainly an investment, but you can customize practically everything, from the arm pads to the casters. It’s available in three sizes, with several options for armrest adjustability, back support, and tilt.

WH Deputy Editor Eunice Lucero-Lee tested the medium-size Aeron in the Jasper colorway for two to four weeks, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. Lucero-Lee, who regularly experiences lower back pain, gave the chair a 5 out of 5.

“This had perfect lumbar support for a whole eight-hour day's work,” she says. She also appreciated the adjustable armrests and how smoothly and quietly the wheels rolled while still offering enough traction and control. (The deep forest green colorway was another bonus.)

Instead of a traditional foam cushion, the Aeron features a breathable mesh seat that offers an almost weightless feeling. And the chair arrives fully assembled—as we'd expect at this price point.

While the steep price tag was Lucero-Lee’s biggest gripe, the Aeron’s customizable fit and excellent lumbar support make it a worthwhile splurge if you spend the better part of your day at your desk.

If you like to lean back and stretch your legs between meetings, the FlexiSpot ErgoX is worth checking out. Beyond customizable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrests, it features an adjustable headrest and a retractable footrest, so you can kick back and put your feet up while catching up on emails or taking a breather between calls.

WH Fitness Reviews Editor Natascha Grief, who already owns a Herman Miller office chair, tested the ErgoX for over a month, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. While she initially found the back support a little uncomfortable, it took about a week for her to get used to sitting in a more upright position.

“I think a good comparison would be switching to a pair of very supportive/corrective shoes after wearing pairs that are less structured,” she says. Once she adjusted to the chair, she liked the firm back support and how the headrest helped her maintain a comfortable neck position.

Grief also loved how comfortable the chair was when fully reclined, though she found the mechanism for pulling out the footrest a little clunky. She ultimately gave the chair a 4 out of 5.

Considering how many adjustments and extras you're getting for the price, the ErgoX is a great option if you prefer a more supportive seat but still want the flexibility to kick back throughout the workday.

Like the Herman Miller Aeron, the Steelcase Gesture comes at a luxury price point, but its sturdy construction, supportive cushioning, and impressive range of adjustments help justify the investment. The chair comes in different materials and colors. Plus you can customize wheels for hard floors or carpet.

Of its many adjustable features, including recline and lumbar support, the most unique is its 360-degree armrests, which allow you to comfortably position your arms whether you're typing on your laptop or scrolling through your phone.

After testing the Gesture for two to four weeks and sitting for two to four hours per workday, WH Managing Editor Laura McLaughlin gave it a 5 out of 5. She loved the firm seat cushion and how the chair managed to feel both stable and flexible.

“The back support specifically feels incredible, with firm yet comfortable padding and adjustable lumbar support,” she says.

At nearly 60 pounds, the chair is on the heavier side, and McLaughlin found it surprisingly difficult to roll around. That said, she felt that its weight contributed to how sturdy and supportive it was.

The Gesture can also support up to 400 pounds, just like the Steelcase Series 2, and is backed by a 12-year warranty, which is reassuring when you're spending four figures on an office chair.

If preserving your home’s interior design is top of mind, then the Branch Verve is minimalist with a unique flair and very comfortable. Made by the same brand as our top pick, this chair is $100 more and has fewer points of adjustment, but it also has a thick seat cushion and a breathable, beautifully designed 3D-knit back that comes in seven chic monochromatic looks.

You can adjust lumbar support, seat depth, and tilt for a decent fit. The chair comes with an optional headrest for $59 more, and the armrests are height-adjustable as well as removable. The chair itself is on the heavier side, weighing in at 40 pounds, but it’s also Greenguard Gold certified, which means it has been tested for volatile organic compounds and chemical emissions.

Read More: Best Standing Desks For Walking Pads

For those who struggle with back pain, a supportive office chair can be the difference between a productive workday and injury. The Steelcase Series 2 is the best option for those folks because it’s weight-activated—you just sit, and the chair’s back tension adjusts to you.

The thick seat cushion relieves pressure, and you can adjust the height, width, and depth of the armrests. (Most office chair armrests are just adjustable by height and sometimes width.) The chair can also support up to 400 pounds, which is about 100 pounds more than most of our picks. In terms of design, you can choose between a variety of colors, two frame colors, an optional headrest, and wheels for carpet or hard flooring.

Read More: Uplift Kneeling Ergonomic Chair Review

At under $500, the HON Ignition 2.0 is a budget office chair that still delivers in terms of support and adjustability. The chair itself is lightweight and easy to maneuver at under 25 pounds, and it sports a simple silhouette that won’t be an eyesore in your home office. The armrests can be raised and widened, and you can also easily adjust lumbar, tilt, and seat depth.

You can also opt to forgo armrests to bring the price closer to $400 or add a headrest and still keep the chair under the $600 threshold. The chair also comes backed by a limited lifetime warranty, which is unique for a high-quality home office chair. (For reference, the warranty on our top pick only lasts for seven years.)

At less than $100, the TikTok-famous Pukami Criss Cross Chair is a great option if you’re furnishing your home office on a budget. The extra-wide, foam-cushioned seat offers plenty of room to sit cross-legged, and its minimalist design and variety of color options make it easy to match with your home decor.

Despite its affordable price tag, the chair swivels, tilts, and can support up to 350 pounds. While it lacks the adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and wheels of our pricier picks, it’s worth considering if you work from home occasionally and don’t want to spend hundreds of dollars on an office chair.

Here are some key features to consider while you search for the best office chair for your body and needs.

Office chairs are not one-size-fits-all, which is why adjustability is crucial. “Adjustability lets the chair match your body so your spine stays in a neutral, supported position,” says Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care. The lumbar support should match the curve of your spine, and your feet should be able to sit flat on the floor, according to Okubadejo.

“An unsupportive chair, or one that does not fit properly, can lead to chronic musculoskeletal injuries over time,” Lees says. “This may lead to pain that persists throughout the day, affecting sleep and stress levels. Long-term injuries may also include nerve damage that can lead to weakness or numbness.”

Most home office chairs are height adjustable and have armrests that can be raised. If a chair has a headrest, which isn’t essential, that may be adjustable as well. “Being able to tweak depth, tilt, and lumbar support prevents hot spots and improves blood flow during long sits.” Okubadejo says. “Small adjustments through the day break up static strain, so muscles don’t fatigue and posture doesn’t collapse.”

Lumbar refers to the lower back, and supporting this curve in your spine can relieve disc pressure and keep your pelvis in a neutral position, according to Okubadejo. “Good lumbar support lowers the risk of stiffness and pain during long hours at a desk,” he says.

Like chair height and seat cushioning, lumbar support will vary by person. “Postural muscles start to relax after a few minutes of sitting,” Lees says. “This leads to added stress on the spinal joints and extremity joints.” Luckily, many office chairs allow you to adjust the height and curve of the lumbar support. Okubadejo recommends options that can move up and down as well as in and out instead of stationary lumbar support.

The main components of a comfortable office chair are a sturdy frame, a thick seat cushion, and a supportive, breathable back. Most office chairs these days have a metal or plastic frame with a foam cushion and mesh back, although you can find upholstered and leather versions.

If you have the opportunity to test chairs in person, make sure that the seat is firm enough for you. “If the cushion is too soft, it won’t offer the support needed over time,” Lees says. “A cushion that is too firm could create pressure points and possibly affect blood flow in the legs.”

The materials of a chair can contribute to its overall weight and weight limit—both of which are important to keep in mind during your search.

Office chairs, like our top pick from Branch, can be beautiful in their own right but not necessarily as stylish as a sofa or armchair. Unfortunately, you may need to prioritize comfort over design when working from home, but you can opt for chairs with upholstery-like materials or lots of color options to marry the two.

Office chairs range in price from under $100 to more than $2,000, but you’ll find that most quality office chairs will cost around $500. It may seem like a lot to spend on a single chair, but it may also be your most-used piece of furniture outside of your bed and mattress if you work from home.

As a longtime remote worker and someone who suffers from chronic back pain, I’m particularly passionate about high-quality office chairs. When I set out to find the best home office chairs, I looked for a variety of models that would suit different body types, from height to weight. Supportive office chairs are easily adjustable, especially when it comes to seat height, armrest height, and lumbar support, so I wanted to highlight chairs that delivered on all three and beyond, with a few budget-friendly exceptions.

My top picks span a wide range of prices, from just $60 to a couple of luxury investment options over $1,500. Whether you’re starting a new remote job or desperately need to revamp your home office, these are the best home office chairs that will keep you comfortable and supported all day long.

#4891. The 5 Best Under Desk Treadmills in 2026, Tested by Certified Trainers

Boost your step count and cardio by walking while you WFH.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

MANY OF US are spending time at a home office for at least a few hours per week these days. Whether it's working your 9-5, surfing the web, or maybe a little gaming, it's become somewhat normal for hours to slip by without moving much more than your fingers on the keyboard. Unless you're making a concerted effort to get your daily steps in, there's a good chance you could use a little help.

But there is hope for breaking up your most sedentary days: a treadmill desk. While it can't substitute for a rigorous workout (say, one on a traditional treadmill), an under-desk treadmill, like the best under-desk exercise bikes, can help you burn calories and get some steps while sending emails, watching TV, or frankly, any otherwise sedentary activity. Plus, most of them fit nicely beneath your favorite standing desk. And no, you don't need to hit 10,000 steps a day to reap the benefits.

A 2021 study found that using a treadmill desk can increase energy expenditure and metabolic rate, and may help prevent the health risks associated with sedentary work environments. So yeah, that means an under-desk treadmill just may help you stay in shape. And no, it's not a substitute for a cardio workout. But hey, getting a little more activity into your day is never a bad thing—and it doesn't hurt to wear walking shoes while doing it, too.

Sitting for extended periods has been linked to various health problems, including obesity, poor posture, musculoskeletal problems, cardiovascular disease, and even diabetes. And upping your daily step count with a treadmill desk is an approachable way to reduce sedentary behavior and its associated health risks.

Increasing your daily movements by even 10 minutes can still make a positive impact on your long-term health. So if you're looking to add an under-desk treadmill to your work-from-home setup, we've got you covered. For the past two years, Men's Health's fitness team has researched and tested over a dozen under-desk treadmills from top home gym and cardio machine brands to find the best treadmill desks to buy in 2026.

Our editors and writers have researched various treadmills and walking pads by conducting market research, scouring forums, and drawing on our in-house team’s knowledge and expertise. From there, we sought to test some models in our office and home offices and to gather the experiences of fellow editors who frequently use walking pads. During our testing, we evaluated each under-desk treadmill on its cost, noise level, size, assembly process, stability, and ease of use. From our findings, we whittled it down to the following guide of the six best under-desk treadmills.

We've been using this walking pad for several months, and it's been a perfect addition to any home office setup. Simple yet effective, the Walking Pad Z1 is a foldable treadmill that weighs 50 pounds, can support up to 242 pounds, and allows for speeds up to four miles per hour, which, for some people, is a light jog.

The relatively narrow width (22 inches) means the Z1 fits under most desks, and the nearly four feet of deck space is long enough to accommodate pretty much any stride length (within the speed range). Our favorite feature is that this treadmill folds completely in half; store it under your couch or bed and simply carry it to where you want to use it.

Again, this is a walking pad, so you won’t get a sweat-inducing workout on it. Also, it can support only people weighing up to 242 pounds. If that’s not you, you’ll want to look for a sturdier option on our list. But to be honest, a brisk power walk is the most that I want to do while writing emails or other work.

The Urevo Walking Pad has proven to be a reliable and financially reasonable way to help me keep my steps up. I like that it’s lasted over two years, is relatively easy to move, and functions as both a walking pad and an under-desk treadmill.

This is a budget pick; the Urevo’s best quality is that it’s a functional walking pad that you can buy for around $200. Mine was bought back in 2022 and used nearly every day for eight months straight. One time, I challenged myself to walk 30,000 steps in a day. I queued up two movies on Netflix and made it through all of The Firm before my wife told me she smelled something burning and I realized the bottoms of my feet were red-hot from two hours and 40 minutes of straight walking.

I’d suggest wearing shoes on this treadmill and not walking on the Urevo for longer than an hour at a time. I hardly use mine as an under-the-desk treadmill (I don’t like typing and walking), but I could as it does fit under my desk. If you’re not buying a standing desk and MacGyver-ing your set-up, measure your desk and Urevo at their widest points to ensure they’re compatible.

All in all, there’s nothing about Urevo that will blow you away. But it is a resilient and affordable walking pad that’ll help you stay active during the winter months and Netflix binges. Is it the cheapest piece of exercise equipment I own? Probably… but I don’t regret the purchase one bit.

There’s no point in buying a commercial-sized treadmill if you plan to get most of your walking done at your desk. The Egofit Walker Pro is a smaller treadmill with a shorter belt and a max speed of 3.1 miles per hour, which is about a 19:21 mile (not fast at all).

At just over three feet long and weighing 48.5 pounds, the Egofit won’t take up much space. According to Amazon reviews, it can be easily stored under your couch or bed. It also has wheels for easy mobility. The Egofit is set at a fixed incline of 5%, which the brand says burns more calories. There’s also an LCD monitor on the front that tracks your pace and steps.

You’re buying a walking pad, not a treadmill. The Egofit can only support up to 220 pounds and won’t do much to enhance your workouts—just your daily activity levels. That said, customers like its size, durability, and maneuverability.

After testing this for a few months, we like to think of this one more as a true walking pad than a treadmill. Ultimately, it has the same function as most under-desk treadmills, but the low-profile aesthetic of the C2 Smart Folding Treadmill can be really attractive.

Especially if you are in an apartment or small office space, the size and look of this design offer significant functional benefits. When you're not using it, simply fold it up and tuck it away. It's not only foldable, but super lightweight, so you can move it from room to room or under the sofa with ease.

It has a maximum speed of 4 mph, so it's great for even fast walkers. A remote control lets you easily adjust the treadmill's speed, switch between modes, and turn it on and off. This makes it easy to customize your workout without stopping or bending down. Buyers have noted the remote battery is not included, so be aware.

The treadmill is also Bluetooth-enabled, so you can pair it with a fitness app while you exercise. But with a weight capacity of just 220 pounds and a compact walking surface, it's not the most suitable choice for bigger or taller guys.

Most of the ultra-budget-friendly models we tested are bare-bones treadmill desks with modest features. The Unsit Under Desk Treadmill is in a class all its own. At nearly $2,600, it's the most expensive model we found. But that premium price tag also sets this one well above every other model in our roundup, too.The wide frame and belt provide 55% more usable walking space. That equates to easier, more comfortable walking with more naturally paced strides to help prevent soreness and injuries. It's also safer, because you're not trying to "fit" your natural gait into an unnaturally small footprint. This model is arguably the quietest on this list—"library quiet," according to Unsit and many reviewers. It's also built with heavy-duty, commercial-grade materials (supports up to 400 pounds) so it's designed to last for years.

It's also the only model we've found with a dedicated smartphone app. It connects the under-desk treadmill to your phone to track steps, distance, calories, and other stats all with a one-touch control setup.

On the downside, that beefy construction makes this the heaviest desk treadmill on this list at more than 160 pounds. We were surprised to find that the maximum speed is only 2 miles per hour. This is definitely more of an under-desk treadmill designed specifically to use while you work, rather than a portable treadmill that happens to fit in your office. Because, really, who is literally running during their hourly Zoom meetings?

This probably goes without saying, but you’ll want to double-check that the treadmill desks you’re shopping for will physically fit your home office. Pay close attention to the overall dimensions, so you can be sure it will fit under your desk. It also helps to have a few feet in every direction around the treadmill to allow enough freedom of movement.

Like all home gym equipment, stability equals safety. You want a treadmill that’s sturdy enough to support you properly. Look for metal frames, which often mean a heavier, more stable construction. If spending a little more money will "upgrade" your purchase from a cheaper, less stable frame to a stronger one, opt for the more expensive option. That increased peace of mind is always money well spent.

If the treadmill desk setup you’re considering includes an attached or complementary desk, be sure it adjusts to a height that’s comfortable for you. Most feature variable table heights, so be sure it can be adjusted to a position that’s ideal for your workflow. Also, treadmills often offer an adjustable speed range, typically in 0.1-mile-per-hour increments. This guarantees the versatility to adapt to your growing fitness needs.

Belt-driven treadmill desks and under-desk treadmill models make noise just like standard treadmills. Not every manufacturer lists the average noise level of its treadmill. But, if a quieter workspace is important to you, be sure to ask or research reviews from other treadmill desk buyers to see what they have to say.

Many treadmill desks require at least light assembly. If you’re not DIY-inclined or just prefer your at-home gym equipment arrive preassembled, check the manufacturer’s website to see just how much assembly is required. In some cases, your retailer may offer assembly, either free or for an additional fee.

These days, many Americans are becoming sedentary. And we know how hard it is to pull yourself away from work, between meetings and deadlines, to go for a quick walk, but treadmill desks offer a solution to that dilemma.

Compared with traditional sitting desks, treadmill desks allow you to increase your physical activity levels while working. This can help improve your cardiovascular health, increase calorie burn, and reduce the risk of chronic diseases associated with a sedentary lifestyle. And who doesn't love a tool that helps you multitask these days?

While research isn't conclusive, some studies have shown that using a treadmill desk can even improve productivity and cognitive function. Walking increases blood flow and oxygenation to the brain, which can enhance mental clarity and focus.

But it is important to note that a treadmill desk may not be suitable for everyone. If you have an existing health condition, it's important to consult a healthcare provider before making any significant changes to your activity levels.

#4890. Hong Kong pushes to bring crypto custodians, advisers under licensing rules

Hong Kong’s securities regulator says the proposal would strengthen investor protections, with the bill set for its first reading in the Legislative Council on Dec. 2.

Hong Kong has published a bill that would bring crypto custodians, advisers and other virtual asset service providers under mandatory licensing or registration, extending oversight beyond trading platforms.

On Friday, the government officially published its Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026, proposing to regulate four activities, including virtual asset dealing, advisory, management and custody. Firms carrying out those activities would need to obtain a license from or register with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).

The proposed amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance would subject providers to fit-and-proper checks and other regulatory requirements. Banks and stored-value facility licensees supervised by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority would also have to register with the SFC to offer virtual asset services.

SFC chief executive Julia Leung said the proposal would strengthen investor protections and provide clearer paths for responsible innovation. The bill is set for its first reading in the Legislative Council on Dec. 2.

In October, Hong Kong said it would introduce legislation covering those four activities before the end of 2026, following consultations on the proposed framework.

The expanded regime has raised implementation concerns. In January, the Hong Kong Securities & Futures Professionals Association warned that introducing licenses without transitional arrangements could force existing businesses to suspend operations while their applications are reviewed. The association called for a six- to 12-month grace period.

Related: Hong Kong adds Hyperliquid to list of ‘suspicious’ crypto platforms

#4889. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.
