#4879. 16 Best Wallpaper Brands to Transform a Room (2026): Editor Picks

Shopping for wallpaper is an excellent way to discover just how indecisive you can be. Between painterly florals, graphic stripes, and whimsical prints, narrowing down the options is practically a full-time job. And that's before you get into the textures, finishes, and the peel-and-stick versus traditional wallpaper debate. There's a pattern for just about every room, taste, and level of commitment. Luckily, we've done some of the research for you.

Wallpaper can also do a lot more than cover four walls. A scenic mural can feel more like large-scale art, and built-in bookshelves can get a refresh simply by lining their backs. Even a drawer lined with your favorite print can be a delightful little surprise, not to mention a low-stakes project for a first-time DIYer. Whether you're ready to commit to an entire room or just want to test the waters, these are the wallpaper brands worth adding to your Pinterest board.

Spin through Spoonflower’s assortment of designs if you’re looking for more impactful wallpaper options. Thanks to graphic designer collaborations with independent artists, this wallpaper catalog includes unexpected patterns (some with a sense of humor!). You’ll also find more traditional floral and graphic patterns, including dreamy prints that hark back to the days of the Great Gatsby.

Consider these pinstripes a subtle way to showcase your team loyalty. This print suits any number of installation methods, whether you prefer peel-and-stick, pre-pasted rolls, vinyl, or grasscloth. There are even metallic accents you can choose for added glamour.

A geometric print awakens a space in a jiffy, and these Bauhaus circles are prime for a midcentury modern abode. Picture it surrounding a fireplace mantle or in an entryway. Adding the print to a ceiling is an unexpected move that gives the space a wow factor.

Wayfair doesn’t miss a thing—hidden amongst their enormous catalog of affordable furniture and decor is a considerable collection of wallpaper. Every print and pattern under the sun is represented here, from chevron to toile to florals.

This tile-inspired temporary wallpaper can work as a backsplash for a “blah” kitchen, on the walls surrounding your soaking tub, or as panels on cabinets. The tiles have a crisp look and, honestly, look pretty close to the real deal.

When in doubt, toile it out. Toile patterns are an easy way to introduce elevated detail. Their classic, subtle details keep things simple, but dynamic. Plus, they work in many different spaces—a bedroom (child or adult), a bathroom, a backsplash, or a living room decorated with early Baroque pieces.

Serena & Lily offers a small, curated collection of nautical, floral, and patterned designs (many that include natural elements like hydrangeas, palm leaves, and sea shells) for dressing up a nursery or bedroom. The color palettes tend to be soft blues, beiges, and variegated greens that play up to the coastal aesthetic.

For Wedgwood fans, this antique-style print is a serene surprise. (Just keep in mind that it’s not removable before taking on a full project.) Pro tip: The brand recommends using a wallpaper liner if you’re working with uneven wall surfaces to keep the finished project smooth.

Here’s another understated option with subtle texture, available in pastels like pistachio, sand, and sky. The muted tones make a great backdrop to any design style, lending the whole room a sense of calm.

While browsing for furniture, we stumbled upon Anthropologie’s robust collection of elevated wallpaper designs that span sophisticated florals and chinoiserie, damasks, and truly special geometric patterns. Their knack for hand-block prints, Renaissance revival, and arabesque designs makes them a no-brainer for any room that you want to be an absolute showstopper. Don’t sleep on their wall murals, too.)

Green bedrooms are trending, but if you want to up the ante on the soothing factor, look no further than this dreamy chinoiserie mural with cerulean-feathered songbirds and lemons to give your space a bit of joie de vivre.

Showcasing Southern artist Jordan Connelly's signature painterly style, these repeating seashells are a non-cliché way to bring a coastal feel to your space. Plus, the tonal color palette makes this great for a child's bedroom or bathroom.

For subtle stripes and vintage-inspired botanicals, McGee & Co.’s small-but-mighty wallpaper selection is there to fulfill your elevated farmhouse needs. Designed to perfectly suit her existing selection of furniture and decor, McGee’s wallpaper serves as a statement finishing touch, one you soon wouldn’t be able to envision your hallway or powder room without. You’ll even find her take on antique Morris and Co. florals through her pastel-hued collaboration.

This moody floral is ideal for crafting a cozy corner in a bedroom or den, especially in the navy colorway. Pair with the matching throw pillows for a pattern-drenching moment.

Sometimes all it takes is a simple stripe to elevate your space. Thanks to its neutral colorway, you can liven it up or tone it down to your heart's content with a blend of upholstery tones, artwork, and decor. Treat it like paint, just with a bit more oomph.

Chasing Paper is our go-to when we want something elevated that has a dash of whimsy. The brand is known for designer collaborations, too. Most recently, Fariha Nasir translated the South Asian art of block printing into wallpaper with floral garlands and tapestry-like designs. All Chasing Paper patterns come in four options: faux grasscloth, performance vinyl, peel-and-stick, and traditional paper. While we checked out samples in all materials, we can vouch for the durability and crisp pattern of peel-and-stick. They also offer tile decals (that happen to work as contact paper to upgrade worn countertops.)

As far as peel-and-stick wallpapers go, the self-adhesive poly-woven fabric of Chasing Paper is second to none. “I am no stranger to putting up peel-and-stick and the Peonies pattern I used for my home office is on par with luxe wallcoverings for heritage brands,” says contributor Yelena Alpert. “The paper adhered securely to the wood paneling, but it had no trouble coming up if I had to realign a panel. The best part is that I did not get any air bubbles—it’s a DIY miracle.” While Alpert opted for the bold red-and-grey colorway that reminded her of Diana Vreeland’s crimson interiors, a toned-down gold-and-cream is also available.

For fans of cabana stripes, this design from Chasing Paper agrees with minimalists and maximalists alike. It’s tough to choose between seven colorways (though we are partial to daisy yellow), which are all great for different purposes: mud rooms, nurseries, beachy bathrooms, or a design-forward living room.

The contemporary meets midcentury aesthetic of West Elm seamlessly carries through to their wallpaper collection, which includes fetching grasscloth designs and designer collaborations, like their latest with design studio Pierce & Ward. Patterns are geometric and playful but not kitschy, and work perfectly for accent walls. You can also find a few animal print designs and artsy figure drawings that are suitable for powder rooms.

Add this organic, playful peel-and-stick wallpaper to your wish list. Those who aren’t homeowners will love how easy the cleanup is for removable wallpaper when moving day rolls around. And when it comes to wallpaper motifs, simple is sometimes better—the soothing neutrals and distinct geometric pattern will elevate and simultaneously calm any room or nook.

Let’s say you want something neutral and textured but grasscloth is not your cup of tea. The Piece & Ward Floral Lattice design is a worthy alternative as it gives the wall a 3D moment but won’t compete with furnishings, especially if you’re into warm wooden pieces. Include ceramic pieces in your home decor to give the entire space a layered look.

The celebrated 19th century British designer, William Morris, was a traditionalist devoted to his craft in the midst of the Industrial Revolution. He taught himself block printing techniques to create more than 20 nature-inspired patterns that encapsulate the Arts & Crafts Movement. His design brand Morris & Co. was established in 1861 and has shown no signs of slowing down as contemporary designers continue to incorporate the wallpaper patterns in their projects. Each wallpaper design is batch-printed in the United Kingdom, making it a good practice to order all rolls at the same time to ensure the dye lots are the same.

The Strawberry Thief is one of Morris & Co.’s most popular patterns and was inspired by the birds that would pop into Kelmscott Manor, Morris’s home in Oxfordshire, to steal the berries from the kitchen. “The gravure printed paper has this heirloom quality that makes it feel as if it is directly plucked from the archives,” says contributor Yelena Alpert, who has samples in indigo and crimson colorways. “Each cheeky bird is about the size of my hand, and the foliage has this watercolor quality. It would look amazing above wood paneling, painted or not.”

Part of the Morris & Co., pattern appeal is that each floral motif is actually on a grid, giving it a certain rhythm. Pimpernel, another favorite, is ornate in the way that the swirls repeat without overwhelming the eye. This design is seen in the Kelmscott House dining room and was chosen by Morris himself. It comes in 16 colorways that span blues, greens, and venture into burgundy.

More than just a place to find scalloped accent chairs and fashion-inspired collaborations (Aimee Song and Carly Cushnie, anyone?), Lulu & Georgia also offers wallpaper. Of course, you can find the likes of Morris & Co. and Scalamandre, but the brand also has their own in-house line. Design stars Sarah Sherman Samuel and Jake Arnold have also lent their talents to this stock with luxe grasscloths and ornate botanicals. Here you’ll find perfect pairings for your velvet bed frame or curved sofa.

Designed by Sarah Sherman Samuel, this intricate print is made more luxe with the addition of a subtle paper weave, adding texture to the linework style drawings.

Polka dots are a playful addition to standard pinstripes, creating a whimsical gateway for those more inclined to traditional styles of design.

Beloved for their quirky paint color names like Disco Nap (a pale acid yellow) and Silver Lake Dad (a stormy blue grey), Backdrop Home also makes patterned wallcoverings that perfectly color-match their hues. Once absorbed into Schumacher’s family of brands, Backdrop also launched archival prints, textured sisal, and peel-and-stick wallpaper options. Backdrop Home offers the kind of whimsical designs that you can’t find elsewhere. Swirling snakes and quilt-like geometric prints that instantly liven up any room, and will have you saying, ‘Oh yeah, that’s Backdrop.’

Taken from the archives of fabric brand Schumacher, Backdrop Home’s iteration takes notes from John Groth’s original 1957 fabric. The sketched horses and riders pair perfectly with the aptly named Ghost Ranch, a warm terracotta-esque brown.

Available in both sisal and plainweave, this geometric print becomes more subtle the more square footage you stretch it across. While wholly impactful in tight spaces like a closet or powder room, this print transforms in large scale, becoming almost hypnotic with its various plum tones.

With a stock full of ornate prints and patterns inspired by historic European textiles, Transylvanian brand Mind the Gap has something for every design style. Heritage-style plaids for the sophisticated sit alongside Eastern-influenced Ikats and jungle motifs for the maximalist. There are also plenty of coordinating textiles if you prefer to pattern-drench your space.

Inspired by upholstery textiles, this maximalist stripe gives the look of fabric-covered walls without the need for a specialty installation.

Vibrant and eclectic, this floral tapestry-style wallcovering recalls early Germanic florals and the brand founders’ childhoods in Transylvania.

York knows wallpaper. The wallcoverings producer has been around for more than 100 years and still dips into the archive to bring back designs from the early 18th century. The Susquehanna Valley, Pennsylvania, factory is the oldest and largest wallcovering producer in the United States. Even if you’re not into heirloom patterns, their designer series includes collections from Magnolia Home, Rifle Paper Co., Missoni, and LoveShackFancy, among many others.

The Italian knitwear company Missoni is now accessible to the more budget-conscious clientele with its new premium peel-and-stick collection (which also includes the iconic zigzags and florals). The Fireworks pattern is almost like a non-dizzying version of the 1990s Magic Eye motif. “I just ordered all three colorways—natural, mauve, and warm grey—to help me decide which one would look best as an accent wall behind my bed,” Alpert says. “Even though it is peel-and-stick, the texture is that of real wallpaper—smooth and velvety!”

A tonal geometric print adds just enough visual interest without overwhelming the eye. This print was designed by Joanna Gaines and the Magnolia Home team to combine the beauty of an artist's sketch with the structure of a true geometric pattern.

Boutique wallpaper brand Hygge & West are beloved for their colorful takes on botanicals and geometric patterns. With best sellers like the Alpine Garden and Bloom, the brand seems to have expertly mastered the ability to create visually striking designs that never overwhelm your space, no matter how small. Even in a powder room, the motifs draw the eye in just the right way, complementing your space instead of taking it over. However, if you’re a maximalist, there are definitely patterns for you too.

The Arcade print blends Pac-Man-like shapes and transforms them into a repeat that’s not dissimilar from a quilt block.

One of the brand’s best-sellers, Alpine Garden’s colors pop against the black background that adds a bit of moodiness to typically saccharine florals.

Not every home comes with a century's worth of character, but that doesn't mean it can't look the part. Best known for its period-inspired lighting and hardware, Rejuvenation brings that same appreciation for Old-World charm to its wallpaper collection. Think intricate botanicals, heritage-inspired prints, and textural takes on grasscloth and sisal that make even a new build feel storied.

Sisal doesn't have to stay underfoot. This Hoffmann print recreates the natural, woven texture in a peel-and-stick wallpaper, bringing instant warmth and dimension to the room.

The soft blue-and-cream palette keeps the Fencott print's small-scale leaf motif from feeling too busy.

Are you more drawn to the cozy, muted tones of winter or the vibrant colors of summer? At Claret & Key, you can have your favorite season on your walls year-round. The brand offers its wallpaper patterns in four seasonal color palettes, each giving the same design a different personality. And if none feels quite right, you can dip into the brand's extensive color library to create a combination of your own. Designs are also available in traditional, heavy-grade, and removable options.

Romeo's hand-drawn leaves give you the look of a custom mural without having to hire an actual muralist. The trailing foliage gives the walls a sense of movement, making this an especially fitting choice for a reading nook straight out of an English country house.

Nellie, on the other hand, brings a little sunshine to the nursery or kid’s room with its vintage-inspired lemon print. The Spring palette reads more neutral, with subdued tones that keep the citrus motif from feeling too playful.

Hang that framed landscape elsewhere—your walls deserve a full view. Crate & Barrel's scenic wallpaper murals turn blank walls into sprawling gardens and leafy landscapes that look as though an artist painted them right onto the surface. Its exclusive wallpaper collection is designed in-house and made in the USA by York Wallcoverings, with plenty of stripes, florals, and textured designs for those who prefer something more understated. If you're having trouble deciding, up to 10 free wallpaper samples should help narrow the field.

There's a reason Jardin has all the charm of a hand-painted landscape—it originally started as one. Painted in watercolor on canvas paper, the tree-lined scene was digitally scanned to preserve every brushstroke and subtle shift in color. The result is a dreamy, softly layered landscape that gives your walls the look of an original watercolor.

Vivaldi puts a wallpaper spin on the classic verdure tapestry. Printed on natural sisal, it even has the texture to play the part.

#4877. A Complete Guide to Caring For Your Nails While Working Out

The gym: Great for muscle tone and cardiovascular health, less ideal for your nails. This advice will help keep your tips in top shape.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat. The one area where a sweat session can fall short, however, is when it comes to the health of our nails.

If you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym. Between chipped polish, cracks and peeling, and the mental gymnastics of trying to avoid both, it can sometimes feel like your nails (and your sanity) are getting a workout of their own. “When I’m lifting plates or handling weights, I’m always conscious of how I’m gripping,” shares celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador Gina Edwards, who's a frequent gym-goer herself. “I use my finger pads rather than the tips of my fingers to help avoid putting unnecessary pressure on my nails.”

Meet the experts: Gina Edwards is a celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador. Dana Stern, MD, is a New York-based dermatologist who specializes in nail disorders. Marisa Garshick, MD, is a dermatologist based in New York City. Jin Soon Choi is a celebrity manicurist in New York City.

Not into manicures? Unfortunately, that doesn't mean you're completely off the hook. Even bare nails can take a beating: “The nail is a thousand times more absorptive of water than the skin,” says New York dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, who specializes in nail disorders. And because frequent handwashing and exposure to moisture often go hand in hand with working out, nails are subjected to expansion as they absorb water and contraction as they dry. “Repeated wet-dry cycles can contribute to splitting and peeling, particularly in people already prone to brittle nails,” Dr Stern adds.

But not to worry—you don’t have to choose between having polished digits and getting your fitness on. With a few smart habits, you can avoid all the pitfalls. Here’s how.

No matter how you choose to work out, there are plenty of ways your nails can suffer. And most of us don't even realize we're putting them in harm's way until it's too late. Maybe you're in a workout class, engaging in some friendly competition with your neighbor to see who can knock out their burpees the fastest, only to jam a nail as your hands hit the ground. Or perhaps the damage happens before you even break a sweat. Picture it: You're pulling on your most compressive pair of leggings when a nail snags on the fabric or, worse, bends backward and breaks.

Of course, some activities pose a more obvious risk than others. Exercises that involve “repetitive gripping, pressure, or friction, such as weightlifting, rock climbing, and certain types of strength training” can be especially hard on your nails, says Marisa Garshick, MD, a dermatologist based in New York City.

Here are a few of the ways your workout routine might be doing a number on them:

Handling dumbbells, weight plates, and other equipment can put pressure on nails, especially if they're long, dry, or already weak, says celebrity manicurist Jin Soon Choi.

Jamming a nail against a hard surface or repeatedly putting pressure on it can cause the nail plate to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis. This can happen to natural nails, too, although extensions may create additional opportunities for snagging.

When a falsie gets caught on something, it can even cause the underlying natural nail to lift from the nail bed, explains Dr. Stern. Depending on the extent of the damage, it can take months for a healthy new nail to grow in.

Frequent handwashing and exposure to harsh cleansers (including those used to wipe down gym equipment and alcohol-based hand sanitizers) can contribute to splitting and peeling, Dr. Stern adds.

While running and cycling may be gentler on your hands, repeated pressure inside athletic shoes can cause bruising beneath the nail (known as a subungual hematoma), thickening, or even nail loss, explains Dr. Garshick.

The good news? Most workout-related nail damage is temporary, provided the nail matrix, which is responsible for nail growth, hasn't been damaged. But more serious injuries can have lasting consequences. A crush injury—heavy weight falling on a nail, for example—could cause permanent damage to the nail matrix, Dr. Stern says. Even when the damage isn't permanent, patience is key. According to Dr. Garshick, fingernails typically take three to six months to grow out, while toenails can take twelve to eighteen months.

The goal isn't to give up your favorite workouts or your favorite manicures. A few tweaks to your nail-care routine and how you handle equipment can make all the difference.

Here's what the pros recommend to keep your nails looking and feeling their best.

This ultra-nourishing product delivers a healthy dose of barrier-repairing ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide sans greasy residue.

Jinsoon Primrose + Honeysuckle Healing Cuticle Oil

Choi recommends this product, from her own line, before bed to help maintain healthy nails and cuticles.

You’ve heard of bond builders for hair, right? This is the same thing, but for nails. It promises longer, stronger nails in just four weeks.

It’s important to keep in mind that Dr. Garshick says not every nail change is workout-related. Persistent discoloration, thickening, or lifting can sometimes indicate a fungal infection, psoriasis, or another nail condition. A new or changing dark streak, particularly one that doesn't grow out, should also be evaluated by a board-certified dermatologist.

At the end of the day, you don't have to choose between crushing your fitness goals and keeping your nails in good shape. In fact, Choi points out that exercise itself can actually be beneficial for nail health, as physical activity promotes healthy circulation, helping deliver oxygen and nutrients to the tissues responsible for nail growth.

It's the accidental injuries and repeated pressure that can cause problems, not the workouts themselves. With a few simple adjustments to your nail-care routine and a bit more awareness of how you're handling equipment, you can keep breaking a sweat without breaking a nail.

#4876. Ivy Shapiro's Manhattan Home is an Artful Ode to Old-School New York

Describing the allure of her sprawling prewar Manhattan apartment, art adviser Ivy Shapiro returns to one theme again and again. “It’s old-school,” she insists. “I have this fantasy that I’m living in a different era. I wanted the apartment to capture this nostalgic vision of old-school New York elegance.” She had plenty to work with. The bones of the unit—its high ceilings, architectural details, and idiosyncratic layout of generous salons and small, meandering rooms—remained largely intact. Major structural alterations were unnecessary to make the space her own, a home that reflects her singular character while graciously accommodating an extensive collection of art that ranges from Stone Age tools and Southeast Asian antiquities to modern and contemporary works created by friends and family.

A Joel Shapiro sculpture holds a corner of the dining room beneath a painting by Aubrey Saget. Works on paper by Edgar Degas and Bob Thompson surmount the fireplace, which is clad in black encaustic tile by clé.

In the living room, a painting by Cecily Brown hangs above a Joel Shapiro table with sculptures by Jonathan Borofsky (left) and Ivy Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson (right), beside a Southeast Asian sculpture. A Jasper Johns lithograph hangs at rear. Sculpture in foreground by Tony Smith.

A Jeremy Anderson chandelier from Gallery Fumi crowns the makeup room. On the wall are works on paper by Cecily Brown.

Shapiro was born into the New York art world of the 1970s, when the artist and collector community had a far different complexion than that of today, a time before “the art world” meant “the art-fair world.” She is the daughter of the late celebrated sculptor Joel Shapiro and art educator Amy Snider, and the stepdaughter of artist Ellen Phelan. Hers is a life organized around and by art, so it is no surprise that the same would be true of her apartment. Here, art is offered the same sovereignty as the home’s human inhabitants, the freedom to take up space, require concessions, demand attention, and even, occasionally, to trip you up. It doesn’t have to fit in above a sofa or over a mantel, nor does it have to stand for something—taste, wealth, a movement, a generation. She accords each piece the independence to exist on its own terms, to be at home.

“I like hanging art in weird places where people don’t like to hang,” Shapiro says. “It’s not an intellectual exercise. It’s more intuitive.”

Architect Raffaella Bortoluzzi, Shapiro’s accomplice in the gentle transformation of the home, drew inspiration from her client’s unconventional sensibility. “I love that Ivy decided not to combine the small rooms and try to impose a more contemporary approach on how the spaces flow. We wanted to respect the historic character and maintain the eccentricities,” Bortoluzzi notes. “Our idea was that every room should have its own little story. We focused on light, playful treatments that in no way fight the original architecture.”

Floating tiled shelves in the kitchen display ceramics by Warren MacKenzie and Shio Kusaka and a small sculpture by Joel Shapiro.

The television room features paintings by Lothar Hempel (left) and Elizabeth Murray (right).

A Joel Shapiro drawing has pride of place in the bedroom of Ivy Shapiro’s son, Walker Crewdson. To the right are a drawing by Sol LeWitt and a Joel Shapiro print.

The television room, for example, is enrobed in aubergine Venetian plaster. The home office, covered in a crimson plaster, features shelves and drawer fronts finished with a surface treatment of crushed eggshells encased in epoxy. Bortoluzzi goosed the primary bath by sprinkling a handful of Piero Fornasetti tiles among a field of pearlescent, zellige-like ones. In Shapiro’s makeup room, ladylike pink plaster walls are amplified by an antique mirror, custom shoe closets with floral fabric behind the glass case fronts, and a sprightly Jeremy Anderson chandelier. “Ivy is very funny and feminine in her way,” the architect says. “The design speaks to those aspects of her personality.”

In the dining room, a Jean Arp collage is installed above an antique tansu with Stone Age tools and Joel Shapiro maquettes.

The last sculpture Joel Shapiro created rests on a table in the primary bedroom. The painting is by Bob Thompson. The sofa is covered in a Rubelli brocade.

Shelves and drawer fronts in the home office are covered in a surface material of crushed eggshells by Nature Squared.

Within the newly refurbished architectural shell, Shapiro deployed her estimable collection of art and objets de vertu with wit and verve. In the living room, the way that Jonathan Borofsky’s bronze Split Head sculpture is balanced by the split-off stone head of an Asian deity feels like a call and response across the ages, as well as a vignette about the endurance of art. They flank a dynamic painting by Shapiro’s friend Cecily Brown like chaperones at an orgy of color and motion. A sculpture by Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson, joins the Borofsky piece atop a table made by her father, one of many Joel Shapiro sculptures, drawings, and maquettes installed throughout the apartment.

A sculpture by Richard Artschwager is installed above a Joel Shapiro bronze in a hallway.

An Axel Salto sculpture sits beneath an artwork by Ryan Sullivan in the living room.

In the hallway to the primary bedroom, a lyrical vintage Danish wall light of abstracted vines, leaves, and flowers hangs above a signature Carl Andre metal floor sculpture, the ultimate butch/femme pairing. In the bedroom itself, a sculpture that Joel Shapiro made in the hospital during his final days (he died in June of 2025) sits inconspicuously on a small table of his own design. It was the last artwork of his storied career.

“Living with so much of Joel’s art, and all these amazing things he and Ellen collected, connects me to [my dad],” Shapiro muses. “The way the apartment is set up, I feel like my life is completely integrated with the art.”

#4874. The 92 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 13 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4873. How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

Strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

“It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” says Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, says Carr.

“They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly important, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” says Carr.

Picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

“They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” says Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” says Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”

Kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

#4871. AD Editors’ Favorite Holcomb Products, Tested and Reviewed (2026)

While lots of homewares cross our collective desks, every once in a while there’s a brand that becomes a hit among our team of (very particular) editors and writers. Holcomb—a Seattle-based maker that specializes in modern hosting essentials like clean-lined carafes and coasters made of natural materials—is one of those brands. Launched in 2021, the brand was founded by father-daughter duo David and Ariel Holcomb who shared the desire to reimagine everyday objects with more beautiful design.

Ever since discovering the brand through a martini team happy hour last fall—where drinks were served in the brand’s Birdie Decanter and charcuterie was sliced with the Wedge Cheese Knives—the wares have been mainstays in our Shop AD staffers’ daily routines and hosting rituals. Shopping editor Audrey Lee uses the handsome salad bowl to showcase her fruit bounty, and contributor Alaina Chou can’t stop gifting the modern coasters, just to name a couple examples. No matter what’s on your shopping list, we think these staples from the brand deserve a place in your home.

A pitcher of water might not be the most thrilling item on your dinner party table, but this carafe gives it a starring role. “Even at a table overflowing with cocktails, I’ve found myself reaching towards the Teeter because it’s so nice to hold,” says shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher. Topped off with a half sphere of ash wood, the slender profile maintains a minimalist look without fading into the background.

Sleek contours, a hand-sharpened, drip-reducing spout, and a wide-mouthed plug-top contribute to this oil can’s “display-worthy design,” according to Chou. She tells us that it’s a breeze to refill, whether it’ll hold the fancy olive oil you brought back from your last trip to Spain or the trusty canola oil you use for everyday cooking.

The brand’s marble spoon rest has taken up primary residence on shopping writer Julia Harrison’s desk since last year, holding a set of steel cocktail picks that keeps her ready for the next happy hour. “It remains on my desk (and not at home) because I like how it looks,” says Harrison. “At any moment I could pour a jar of olives out for snacking, or spear one on a cocktail pick for a cheeky after-work martini.”

Two Shop AD team members are fans of Holcomb’s mortar and pestle: Arzbaecher and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker. “I want to be the kind of home chef that regularly busts out a mortar and pestle to grind fresh spices and herbs with an Ina Garten–level ease,” says Arzbaecher. “This one has called me to task ever since it entered my kitchen cabinet.” Baker says the durable granite bowl is especially handy for mashing avocados to prep guacamole and grinding coffee beans. Nestled inside a cutout wood frame, the mortar and pestle make heirloom-worthy additions to any countertop.

Another fan favorite, the Puddle coasters are Chou’s go-to gift when she’s out of ideas. Describing them as “modern but timeless,” she appreciates that the design’s slight lip catches any beverage run-off and errant drips. Baker gives credit to the giftable coaster set for keeping her coffee table free of water marks, similarly praising the sleek look and raised edges for containing condensation.

Lee uses the Dot Salad Bowl to hold her ever-changing fruit bounty. “This handsome wooden bowl has been permanently fixed on my dining table since receiving it a year ago,” she says. Lee styles the bowl’s matching walnut cover underneath as a base to the vessel, something she says gives the decor piece a more grounding presence. “Every morning I grab some citrus or a banana before heading out the door, and this is 100 times nicer than the glass Pyrex I was previously using.”

This knife trio is perfect for wine and cheese at golden hour, especially since the frosted handles emit a slight glow when they catch the light. “The green hue would look extra charming against a cheese board,” insists contributor Lori Keong, who plans on practicing her charcuterie skills with this colorful set during holiday hosting season. “I’m lactose intolerant, but a girl can still dream….”

#4870. 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

Whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” says global editorial director Amy Astley. “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!”

We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD-approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present.

There are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home. Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley says in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors.

Created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work.

Global features director Sam Cochran’s debut coffee table book opens with the words, “Nothing is interesting unless it is personal.” His project, American Designers at Home, brings that idea to life beautifully. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—says, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur.

Levasseur says that Simon Upton’s most recent release with Rizzoli contains “beauty and poetry on every page.” The title is a nod to the iconic London A–Z: The detailed street atlas that every Londoner seemed to own in the 1980s and early 2000s, pre-Google Maps. Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.”

This beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” says senior digital editor Catherine Hong. “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration."

“Whether or not you’d ever dare to decorate with Sasha Bikoff’s over-the-top flair, this book is guaranteed to make a splash on your coffee table,” says Hong. Behind its trippy, hot-pink cover lies screaming color, clashing eras, and utter fantasy. The designer lives by her “Rule of Three Wows”—chronicled in the pages—and her book is, accordingly, loud, wildly fun, and a little bit insane in the best way.

Studio Valle de Valle’s debut monograph offers a refined window into the AD100 firm’s singular vision and creative evolution—surveying 10 projects from the past 10 years. Printed in Italy, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson, the pages demonstrate the firm’s interior philosophy of creating spaces that feel personal, layered, and deeply inhabitable. “The edition isn’t just a tour de visual force, it’s an art object unto itself,” says Cochran. “I would expect nothing less from these brilliant auteurs."

“One of Meyer Davis’s greatest strengths is how cofounders Will Meyer and Gray Davis distill references, ideas, and desires into a highly refined vision,” says AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach. As client Jenna Lyons puts it in the book’s foreword, “They gave me clarity.” Beyond a printed body of work, The Language of Home is a testament to the collaborations that shape the studio's warm, reductive interiors. Designed with honest materials and a contemporary lens, the featured residences—a modern glass house in the Berkshires and an earthen dwelling in Puerto Escondido—reflect their inhabitants with a calm, clear ease.

The inaugural monograph from AD100 design duo Humbert & Poyet showcases their signature brand of eclectic French luxury, blending Art Deco glamour, midcentury modernism, and the decorative arts. Spanning residential and hospitality projects around the world, the book by AD contributing editor Gay Gassmann takes readers from a French Riviera villa to a Milan restaurant housed in a 17th-century chapel, with stops in New York, Paris, Monaco, and Seoul.

In New York: Atelier AM, Alexandra and Michael Misczynkski, the married couple behind the AD100 firm, shine a light on their New York projects, all beautifully captured by François Halard. Spotlighting a range of projects like elegant Manhattan residences and more relaxed Long Island retreats, contributor Ingrid Abramovitch says the book itself is “equally exquisite, with a cover resembling wood grain, and high-gloss pages printed in Italy.”

2026 AD New American Voices honoree Amber Guyton first burst onto the design scene by way of her hit blog, Blessed Little Bungalow. “Her debut book brings the same wit and spirit to the printed page in a kaleidoscope of color and pattern,” says Cochran. Senior shopping editor Nashia Baker adds that the pages “truly embody how to bring personality to any room.” Throughout the book, she makes a case for maximalism, and distills her approach into four pillars: joy, culture, layers, and intention.

“This book is perfect for cinephiles, design-lovers, or anyone with a case of wanderlust,” says senior digital editor Rachel Wallace. Film is one way to travel the world without ever leaving the sofa, and with her new project On Location, longtime AD contributor Cathy Whitlock takes readers on a global cinematic journey. The book goes behind the scenes of films that make you want to hop on a flight and never look back. Colorful Mexico City scenes from Frida and Marie Antoinette’s famous Palace of Versailles shooting location are both represented.

Organized by a series of chapter essays rather than specific projects, AD100 designer Dan Fink’s debut book explores bigger questions on how spaces, objects, and compositions move us across time. At the same time, the book spotlights several career-defining projects from his namesake studio, including previously unpublished interiors like Manhattan penthouses, Hawaiian beach retreats, Hollywood homes, and more.

One of the few completely fail-proof gifts is one of the best coffee table books of the season—weighty tomes whose thick, glossy pages feature stunning photographs and illustrations, to be specific. On a superficial level, they add ambiance, whether you place them in a library or a living room. But the best ones live in your home forever, while expanding your horizons far beyond. They also come across as far more memorable and thoughtful than the expected candle or bottle of champagne. Like works of fiction, there are limitless topics that can make deciding on an eye-catching hardcover (that doubles as home decor) seemingly impossible.

But that’s where we come in. Our team has gathered its favorite giftable recommendations for everyone from tennis enthusiasts to globe-trotters to interior design aficionados. From a book focused on hotels around the world to another that spotlights Tokyo style, there are plenty of ways to adorn the coffee tables of all the people on your holiday gift list. Most of them came out in 2024, but we’ve also included a few evergreen picks that make worthy gifts any year.

Plus, if you’re down to the wire on last-minute gifts, rest assured that most of these selections are available (and even marked down ahead of the holidays!) on Amazon.

Après-ski style needs no introduction in a season full of fuzzy Fair Isle sweaters, but it’s the cozy interiors of the chalets along the world’s most popular ski slopes that are worthy of a second look. From the wooden beams of an A-frame to the blazing fireplaces set within them, AD contributor Kathryn O’Shea-Evans pores over the finer details in this fun, wintery escape.

As associate digital editor Maya Ibbitson previously described it, “Alpine Style is a true compendium of resort luxury,” spanning spectacular chalets from Gstaad to Aspen and featuring the works of AD PRO Directory members such as Massucco Warner, Robbins Architecture, and Kara Adam Interiors.

Japan’s interiors are a perpetual reference for modern-day designers, and whether you’re a proponent of wabi-sabi principles or just looking for small space ideas, Tokyo Style will help you explore both.

Originally published in 1993, it’s since become a collector’s item and cult classic, and it was recommended by commerce writer Julia Harrison for anyone who would appreciate a more intimate glimpse of Tokyo’s dwellings: “Apartamento, an imprint that consistently delivers on elite design, has reintroduced Tsuzuki’s collection for us to enjoy in its full brilliance—that is, not a ‘fine’ condition original at $170 with $90 shipping from eBay.”

Prefaced with a foreword by Spike Lee, BLK MKT Vintage peers into the world of the Brooklyn antique shop’s endlessly curious founders Jannah Handy and Kiyanna Stewart. “This monograph teems with more than 300 studies of vintage ephemera and reads like a collage with context, or an I spy for your inner adult archivist,” writes Ibbitson of the book. For collectors, Sydney Gore pinpoints it as a must-have for your rotation.

Donald Judd’s considered, minimalist approach to design has fostered its own cult of acolytes who, these days, emulate his daybeds and chairs on Instagram.

For the true Juddheads, the Judd Foundation has produced a new book edited by his children Rainer and Flavin Judd that chronicles more than one hundred of his functional works produced between 1970 and 1992. “Mixed in are the juiciest bits: photos from past and present of those pieces in Judd-designed spaces in New York and Marfa,” Ibbitson writes.

AD’s Milan correspondent Laura May Todd penned a delightful homage to Italian living this year, one which spans from historic palaces in Venice to the homes of creatives like Luca Guadagnino along with midcentury Milanese apartments, so you can enjoy a small taste of la dolce vita on each page.

It was one of the AD PRO team’s favorite book releases this fall, one which should suit the person on your list who never got over their Italian study abroad or is manifesting a Sicilian villa in their future.

For the person on your list who delights in having people over, How They Entertain, released this fall, serves as a comprehensive guide to (and celebration of) the art of hosting.

Written by Pierre Sauvage, it’s chock-full of inspiration for your next dinner party, from recipes to design notes on arranging a tabletop to remember, as well as interviews with tastemakers like Laura Gonzalez about their particular philosophy on entertaining guests.

Considering this year’s smash summer hit Challengers and the enduring popularity of tenniscore (polos, skorts, and all), it’s clear that tennis is a lifestyle that has captured the imagination of many people, avid tennis players or not.

This book recommended by the AD PRO team earlier this year is dedicated to a more, uh, underserved cross section of the sport: the backdrops where athletes volley their way to tournament glory (clay, grass, asphalt, and beyond) in locales from Queens to Kenya.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent is no stranger to the pages of this very magazine, and his new book is a friends and family affair studded with stars, like Oprah and legendary choreographer Fatima Robinson, with whom Brent has formed close connections over the past 20 years.

We’ve previously described the book (layered with sentimental photos and new snapshots of contributors in their home) as “more scrapbook than design manifesto, a love letter to the spaces that people have inhabited and inherited over the years.” Read AD’s extensive interview with Brent for more backstory behind (and tidbits from) the book.

For art buffs with a fondness for the Harlem Renaissance—an era synonymous with greats like Aaron Douglas, known as the father of African-American art—this new book compiled by MoMA curator Denise Murrell is an excellent title to know. “Having this book is about as close as you’ll ever get to owning one of the original masterpieces featured in the Harlem Renaissance exhibition at The Met,” Gore says.

Self-interested plug here, but we really couldn’t publish a guide to coffee table books without mentioning our own, AD at 100: A Century of Style. For the design buff with an appetite for lush interiors and a healthy curiosity for how A-listers live, there’s no more satisfying holiday treat than this tome that delves into the homes of the Obamas, David Hockney, Diana Vreeland, and beyond. It also serves as a bird’s eye view of a century in design and architecture, including the works of Frank Gehry, David Hicks, Frank Lloyd Wright, and much, much more.

Architecture has a reputation for myopia when it comes to its foremost voices, but this book seeks to rectify the past with a fresh overview of some of its most brilliant underrepresented talents, including interviews with female architects around the globe such as Tatiana Bilbao, Liz Diller, and Julia Gamolina.

“100 Women offers a refreshing reframe of the built environment outside of the male-dominated Western canon, proving the benefits of sourcing alternative points of reference,” Ibbitson wrote of it in AD PRO’s guide to the best new design books out this past spring.

Colony founder Jean Lin has mentored and platformed some of the design world’s brightest rising stars, and in her first book out this year, she tapped a wide pool of creatives to explore the concept of collections that inform their work, from ceramicist Stephanie H. Shih’s cache of soy sauce bottles to Mira Nakashima’s stockpile of lumber inherited from her father, architect turned furniture maker George Nakashima.

That’s just one facet of the book Ibbitson previously described as an “encyclopedic, elemental study of artist studios, profiles, materials, and everything else under the design umbrella,” with plenty of wisdom imparted within its pages, from how-tos to styling tips. Read our interview with Lin for more of her notes on curating a collection of your own.

Luna Luna—a 1980s artist-led amusement park featuring works by icons of the art world such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Salvador Dalí, and David Hockney—is experiencing a resurgence as of late, what with a new retrospective at The Shed this year, along with a revival of the park itself in Los Angeles late last year.

This 2023 book takes a deeper dive into Luna Luna’s history blending fine art with the playful energy of a carnival—encompassing rides, interactive installations, and surreal sculptures. It comes recommended by associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz, who nods to the book’s breadth of archival media within, from photos to sketches, that are accompanied by behind-the-scenes stories.

For jet-setters who love to live large on vacation, Spencer Bailey’s Design: The Leading Hotels of the World (released just this month) is one sure way to sustain a sense of wanderlust. His new book takes readers on a visual journey to 80 countries around the globe, inviting them to mentally book into sumptuous spaces from The Okura in Tokyo to the Portrait Hotel in Milan. It’s rounded out by notable travel and design writers like Maria Cristina Didero and Mark Ellwood, who lend us their travel tips, on top of their reflections on the lodgings featured within.

Whether the view outside the window is of the Santa Monica pier or the peak of Mount Rainier, the homes AD’s most trusted interior photographers on the West Coast shoot always end up looking as impressive as the scenery that surrounds them. While many of them are bicoastal or even work internationally, these pros are experts on shooting West Coast interiors. And they’re not just leading lights in the field of interior photography; many of these artists excel in travel, landscape, or portrait photography as well—but each one of these photographers is guaranteed to make a home look like a worthy setting for a Hollywood blockbuster.

Step inside a Beaux Arts San Francisco home designed by Jonathan Adler.

A midcentury Bay Area home gets a Japandi-inspired renovation courtesy designer Cathie Hong.

A little guest enjoys a big room at Kisawa Sanctuary in Mozambique.

Peter Baker’s interest in the built world continues long after a commission wraps. The Los Angeles photographer pairs interiors work for talents including Martha Mulholland and Alexander M. Liberman with an extensive fine art practice exploring his surroundings.

A subdued palette allows scenic views to remain the focus in this West Coast condo.

A media room layered in Orior furnishings

Known for her artistic commercial work, which centers on architecture and interiors, Elizabeth Carababas produces shots with a strong scenographic sense—one gets the feeling that the inhabitant is just outside the frame.

AD100 design firm Pierce & Ward crafted a California cottage with Scottish charm for actor Karen Gillan.

Justin Chung’s photos are as sunny as California itself. He captures the state’s famous light masterfully as it illuminates residences with its warm glow, showcasing the best of LA living.

The bathroom in a 1927 home in Los Feliz designed by Daphne Nauleau

Michael P.H. Clifford has landed multiple cover stories in top design publications, including AD’s May 2024 issue with Emma Roberts, and has a knack for capturing people naturally yet strikingly within their homes.

Step inside Louisa Pierce’s century-old Tudor in Birmingham, Alabama.

Ty Cole adroitly navigates a wide array of clients, from architecture firms to corporate behemoths including PNC Bank and Morgan Stanley. He’s also a treasured collaborator here at AD and has contributed to Domino, Fortune, and Departures, among others.

Designer Melissa Benham revitalized this home in the Hollywood Hills.

Natural light floods this living room in Rancho Mirage.

The quiet, contemplative interiors that Bess Friday has captured while working all over the world have appeared in AD, as well as in House Beautiful and Elle Decor. From beachside bungalows to Parisian apartments and French chateaux, her architectural subjects are always shown in their best light.

Designer Heidi Caillier’s home in San Francisco

A Beverly Hills home designed by Suchi Reddy

A crisp white dining room captured by Tessa Neustadt

Designer Gille Mills created this living room in Hollywood.

In each of her shoots for AD, Jenna Peffley has been able to convey the personality of the home and its occupant to a T—be it Miley Cyrus’s bold and boisterous playground, Colman Domingo’s sunny modernist digs, or Orville Peck’s rustic tree house.

A former model who worked with the likes of Richard Avedon and Mario Testino, Resen moved behind the camera shooting fashion and travel as well as interiors. Having been an art director and magazines including Vogue, and publishers such as Rizzoli, Resen brings an editorial eye to every project.

A bedroom in Beverly Hills by Simo Design

Jessica Sample’s portfolio could keep an interiors lover and a travel obsessive equally occupied. The Los Angeles photographer shoots homes and hotels alongside far-flung destinations, with collaborators including House of Honey, Simo Design, and Hammer and Spear.

Interiors by Lauren Nelson and Meredith Dunn, of Lauren Nelson Design

A resident of the Bay Area who also works out of the Big Apple, Seth Smoot is the eye behind these light-drenched photos of Sweet July, Ayesha Curry’s store and event space. His partner Kendra, a stylist, is a frequent collaborator.

Inside the brick-walled home of a collector

Photographer Jake Stangel has taken on a range of commercial and editorial clients, from The California Sunday Magazine to Heath Ceramics. A dual citizen of the US and Canada who also holds visas to work in China and Brazil, Stangel is a colorful collaborator who might even bring a Doja Cat–and–Four Tet–studded Spotify playlist to your next shoot.

Inside stylist extraordinaire Colin King’s light-filled Manhattan loft

Rich Stapleton’s photographs offer a moment of calm and reflection. His focus on discovering and highlighting details reveals a process that involves truly understanding what makes a space unique and then tracing a personal narrative through a series of images.

This spa-like bathroom in San Francisco was designed by Noz Nozawa.

For anyone keeping tabs on the Bay Area’s expressive interiors, Christopher Stark’s collaborator list should ring a few bells. Ken Fulk, Jay Jeffers, Noz Nozawa, and Jon de la Cruz have all worked with the San Francisco photographer.

A full-floor unit in the Sherry-Netherland apartments in New York, designed by Martin Brûle

From Frank Gehry to Giancarlo Valle, Christopher Sturman’s subjects cover quite the architectural spectrum. Working between Los Angeles and New York, he has also photographed projects involving Renzo Piano and Clements Design.

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

A globally inspired interior captured by Teal Thomsen

Texas-born and California-based, Teal Thomsen possesses a deep appreciation for the American West. That’s clear in her photography, which features plenty of natural light and warm earth tones.

Delivering inviting shots for editorial and commercial clients alike, Madeline Tolle has produced a number of shoots for AD, including the LA pad of actor Jesse Tyler Ferguson.

A photo showcasing the Pira G2 system bookshelf by String Furniture

Pia Ulin knows her way around a camera—and clay. The photographer and ceramicist works between Los Angeles and Stockholm, with Halleroed and Lotta Agaton Interiors among her collaborators and IKEA and String Furniture in her campaign portfolio.

What happens when a documentary photographer spends time with a landscape studio? Will Warasila’s 10 Days with Terremoto photo series offers one answer. Based between Montana and Los Angeles, he looks beyond buildings to the people shaping their surroundings.

#4865. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.
